Warrington, May 10th, 1892. VALUATION OF SHOP AND WAREHOUSE, &e., situate In Horsernark et-street, belonging to Messrs. W. P. and W. Skelton, Limited. Having inspected this property, I beg to report us follows, viz. The whole of the premises cover enema of 498 square yards, or thereabout, and is freehold subject to an annual rental of £75.• payable to Lord Winmarleigh. The main building covers an area of about 262 square yards. It is three storeys high, with good basement under the whole area, and attic formed in root. The shop has a frontage to Horsemarket-street of 56 feet, and a clear depth back of over 42 feet ; the two show rooms above are the same size. The property is well anti substantially built, and I. eom- para,ively new, having been erected only five years. In addition there is a good yard. about two-thirds of Which is covered with glass, also a two storey warehouse adjoining same. I estimate the value of the whole property to be five thousand and anti hundred pounds.
Yours truly, JOHN EDWARD WRIGHT. Surveyor and Valuer. Warrington. _

Tea si za Sir Andrew Clarke. For years. whenever my Customers have asked me for a Mild Tea, I have advised the Pure. old Fashioned China which I keep, end the advice has been appreciated. It is very satisfactory to them that such an eminent authority as Sir Andrew Clarke, the London Physician, corroborates *pi nion
Here is an extract from an Interesting lecture, delivered by Sir Andrew the other day, to the Students of the London Hospital:

" Tea lea blessed beverage. Ido not know what I should do without 14_ But there is tea and tea, an.l one of the teas I have in my mind is the representatbvi of all that is phvsiologleally wicked. Igo about town a good deal holding consulta- tions here and there, and about five O'clock, when I get into a place, the lady of the house will say to me : 'Sir Andrew, you look tired, do let me give you a cup of tea.' I say ' thank you very much.' But the tea has stood for half-an-hour, and she remarks, 'I know you do you not like it strong, Sir Andrew.' and she then pours about a tablespoonful of the tea into a cup and tills thecup up with water. Noy I call it positivecruelty to give tea like that to anybody and I hope you, gentlemen, will always set your face against it. Tea, to be useful, should be first of all Black China Tea ; the Indian Tea which is being cultivated has become so polwertni in its effects upon the nery ms system that a cup of it taken early in the morning, as many do, so disorders tin nervous system that those who take It actually get into a state of tea intoxication, and it produces a form of nervous disturbance, which is most painful to witness. If you want to have, either for yourselves or for your patients, tea which will not Injure and which will refresh, get. Hiack China Tea, putting in the right measure—the old fashioned tens pooktul for each person and one for the blessed pot. Then pour on briskly boiling water, and within five minutes you must pour It Of again, or it will become wicked instead of good." - - - • - • • •

PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS. IT is only the man with a pocketful of rocks who can afford to throw stones. Ir is said that a young lady and the mirror sometimes make a nice little mutual admiration society. WHY should a common soldier, who has been in the ranks a long time, be afraid to meet an excise officer? Because he's a private still. ONE of the best-looking girls in the Tioy Seminary is a red-haired girl of Vermont. Out of compliment to her hair, they call her the "torch of love." Too much study is said to affect the mind. A teacher, of our acquaintance, says that he knows a number of cases where it would affect very favour- ably, too. TALKS ON ART.—He—"HOW lovely Miss De Long looks; she reminds .nre of an old picture." Rival beauty—" Yes, a very old picture, and restored." COUNTRY Baton (looking over bill of fare)— " John„what's Patty de fee grass?'" Groom —" 'Sh ! Don't talk so loud, or people'll think we're ignorant. It must be French for celery." As the convalescent patient said to the doctor when an extravagant bill was presented, " What's the use of your saving my life, if you shoVe a bill at me afterwards so big that I worry myself to death over it? JOHNNIE—" Mamma, when I grow older shall I be bald?" Mrs. Brown —"I don't know." Johnnie—" I hope I 5h,11." Mrs. B.—" Why ?" Johnnie—" Because then I can sit in the front row as the other old men do." • A FAnmEn in Hampshire recently forwarded a letter to a neighbouring town, requesting the post- master to deliver it "to any respootable attorney." After ten days it was ieturned with the significant indorsement: "Neale hero." "PA, has the world got a tail?" asked an urchin of his father. "No, child," replied the father; " how could it have one when it's round ?" "Wall, why do the papers say, 'so wags the world,' if it hasn't got a tail to wag ?" Toz following toast was lately given at a 'bach- elors' dinner, and drank with enthusiasm: " The Ladies' Nails—may they always be on hand, but never come up to the scratch.' Yorrso HOUSEKEEPER, after gazing helplessly at the different " cuts " in a butcher's—' I want a piece that I can use for soup." Butcher—" People generally get fore-legs for soup, ma'am." Young housekeeper, aghast—" How many did you say— four ?" • •

WOMAN (begging) —" Won't you help a poor woman who has been left alone in the wide, wide world ?" Sailor (who has been shipwrecked)— "That's nuthin', mum. As an instance of the carelessness of the public in leaving their portable property in public places. it may be mentioned that on Saturday last a ladx tpplied for a lost umbrella at the Lost Propertf Office, Scotland-yard, and, on its being restored to her, went away leaving behind her another um- brella and a brown paper parcel.

While the economic changes prop:,sed n d ap- proved by the Trade Union Congress overshadowed everything else in the debates we should not over- look the important political reforms which it advocated. No subject was -received witb more cordiality and unanimity, for instance, than the payment of members. The discussion on labour representation turned mainly on this reform.

Some sixteen pages of the new issue of the "Strand Magazine " are devoted to an account, pic- torial and descriptivek of the Queen's dolls: Miss Frances Low, the writer, has had the privilege of spending an hour among the dolls, many of them clothed by her Majesty's own hands, with which the Queen played as a child. Her Majesty has given, though Sir Henry Ponsonbyotne particu- lars for publication about these dolg, and has taken the trouble to make a few autograph notes to the article.

" G.A." writing to the " Star " thus hits off The Costers' Modest Demand ": We want no shops superb, All we want's a bit of kerb, Just a little bit of roadway in the mud, Just a little bit of road When our goods can all be showed; But they nips our speckerlation in the bud. Then we're had up afore the beak, And we ain't allowed to speak, And the magistrates they give us all a wiggin' ; When our living we can't get, There's a certain clever set As is really quite surprised we take to priggin'.

Dispite all assertion to the contrary, the Duke of • York is engaged to frincess May. It would have been formally announced some time sin6e had not the .Queen, wha, as is well known, holds vsfrong views on, mourning observances, objected. It is probable now that no official declaration will be made until at least twelve months have elapsed since the Duke of Clarence's death. Meanwhile, , however, preparations are being quietly made for the marriage' which, it is expected, will folio* very I closely upon the formal intimation of the engag.,- nient; and, what is perhaps more significant, the question of the disposal of the wedding presents sent to Princess May at the time of her engagement to the Duke of Clarence if allowed to remain dormant.

Besides Dr. Talmage, the City of Paris, whicll sailed early on Wednesday for New York, has several well-known people among her passengers. There is for instance, T. B. Aldrich, the American poet, who, with Mrs. Aldrich, has been in this country for a couple of months. Mr. Aldrich is one of our most regular Transatlantic visitors, and this summer -other prominent American writers--Mr. Frank Stockton for one—have also been here. Mr. Henniker Beaton, M.P., who knows America almost as well as he knows Australia, is also going over by the City of Paris. So are Lord and Lady BraYe and the Hon. Everard Fielding, brother to Lord Denbigh, all of these being bent on a trip to Japan and round the world.

A. present from the gods! They don't come often, and when they do, deserve notice. Colonel Maple- son is the recipient. A few months ago this Shin- in g light of Italian Opera was robbed of his watch- chain in Drury Lane, and, not being a gentleman ot retiring disposition. he mentioned it freely. The news even reached San Francisco, where gold watch-chains are more indispensable indications of respectability than they ere here, and now Colonel Mapleson has received a chain of gold quartz, with an unsigned note stating thett,it is the gift of the gods of San Francisco, who cannot forget the man who gave America its greatest musical enjoyment in the present generation. It is an appropriate gift. The god of San Francisco is gold.

Did Napoleon 111. put rouge on his face to con- ceal its paleness on the fatal day for his country and his dynasty when he surrendered his sword at Sedan to his" good brother" the King of Prussia? The subject is still being hotly discussed in France a propos of M. Zola's novel "La Debacle." M. Zola, • whose painstaking minuteness is well known, declares—it will be remembered—he has positive evidence that the Emperor did paint his cheeks: Princess Matilde has, it appears, related the story more than once. Oil the other hand, M. Faul de Cassagnac comes forward to champion his late master' Ile accompanied the Emperor during the whole of the day of the surrender, and is guitb cer- tain that the story of the rouge is an invention. There the matter rests, and the historian of the future must take his choice of the two versions. '

The Bishop of Chester is going ahead with his model public-house scheme. He intends to draft a Bill on the subject and introduce it next session. What the Bishop wants is that the town and county councils should control public-houses in the same way as they would run schools or any other insti- tution for the good of the community. The Bishop starts on the assumption that pubs are necessary, and are not in themselves an evil. The local authority would settle the number of pubs which qmght to exist in a district, hours of opening, &e. The system would also lead to the stoppage of adul- teration. The system would also lead to the stop- page ot adulteration. The Bishop expects that opposition will come from the teetotalers and the trade, and what he wants to see is a wave of enthusiasm which will carry the moderate drinker with him. He is waiting for that wave, but it does not seem to be in any burry to come along.

Mr. Lahouchere, in his gaily irresponsible posi- tion, has been laying down the Radical program for next session. As the present Ministry have attained to power by Radical support he hopes that they will go in for Radical measures, which include a policy of non-intervention in foreign affairs, especially in Egypt. Speaking for the Radicals, Mr. Labouchere says," We want to see the present disfranchising legislation laws" swept away, "we want our villagers to be masters in their villages,' and to see full justice done to "the rights and requirements of labour." "We want the hideous monopoly of the brewers to cease without a farth- ing of compensation." These and other reforms the new Parliament will have to pass, and Mr. Labou- chere, with other Radicals, regrets that an autumn session has not been held, so that some progress could be made with the great budget of legislative proposals which have been formnlated or shadowed forth.

Lord Rosebery's reference on Saturday evening to the prominence that colonial intelligence is gain- ing in the columns of the London Press is a remin- der of his own tour through Australia and New Zealand a few years ago. Perhaps the greatest ovation of the tour was on the °occasion when Lord and Lady Rosebery came to the Melbourne Athen- mum to distribute prizes to the pupils of the Scotch College. Young Caledonia in the colonies cheered itself hoarse that day. Another interesting incident occurred during Lord Rosebery's address to a num- ber of working-men from Collingwood, a Radical suburb of Melbourne, that will live in history as the first constituency to send a labouring man to a British Parliament. One sturdy artisan got so enthusiastic over Lord Rosebery's progressive de- mocratic sentiments that be cried out, " Resign your earldom and become our member." Lord Rosebery was so tickled by this interjected sugges- tion that it was some time before he could resume his speech.

Mrs. Garrett-Anderson, M.D., gave a charming garden-party on Saturday at her country residence, West Hill, Aldeburgh. Rain threatened, but held off obligingly for Mr,Alfred Capper's al fresco thought- reading entertainment in the grounds, where also light refreshments were served. The youth,beauty, and fashion of Aldeburgh came in their brightest and best, and the golfing element was largely repre- .,ented. Among the celebrities present were Miss ' Philippa Fawcett, in a pretty ivory gown her mother, Mrs. Fawcett; Mr. Philip Cowell, this year's senior wrangler; and several lady doctors. Some clever amateurs, Mrs. J. Davidson and her daugh- ters, played the intermezzi from `• Cavalleria Rusticana " and " L'Amico Fritz " in the white- panelled drawing-room, and Mr. Charles Ganz sang Schumann's "Two Grenadiers." Then everybody went away, and the surgeon hostess hurried away to visit a poor boy in a back street, whose femoral artery had been severed some days previously by a broken bottle thrown at him in a frolic. Messrs. Macmillan and Co. are issuing an edition of Dickens which is likely to be exceedingly popu- lar. The volume to hand is "The life and, adven- tures of Martin Chuzzlewit," and it is a .reprint of the first edition, with illustrations, .and a bio- graphical introduction by Mr. Charles Dickens the younger. There is a reproduction in facsimile of the wrapper of the original edition, in which the story is given as "edited by Boz, with Illustrations by Phiz." This bringing together again of author and artist, two men of great genius in their several ways, makes this edition all the more acceptable to the public. In his introduction Mr. Charles Dickens the younger gives a number of interesting details of the circumstances under which "Martin Chuzzlewit" was written and published, and quotes his father as speaking of this novel as containing the best of his writing. It is interesting to note that no fewer than five plays have been founded upon 'Martin Chuzzlewit." It may be added that the volume is handsomely bound in green cloth, and published at 3s. 6d. "A First Family of Tasajara " is the title of a new novel published by the same firm, from the pen of Bret Eiarte. Like all his stories, it abounds in vigorous descriptive writing, and the characters are as striking as they are well drawn. There is not much evidence of plot in the first portion of the story, but that is the art of the writer in seeking to conceal his art, for, as is seen later on, every chapter has been written with a view.to the final development, which is thoroughly realistic, while out of the ordinary run. If," A first family of Tasajara " does not add to Bret Harte's reputation, it certainly sustains it, and that is saying a great deal. " The new House cf Commons," price Is., is a hand- book of Over 300 pages, also published by' Messrs. Macmillan and Co. It has been reprinted from the "'rimes," and contains, along with reliable biographical notices of members of Parliament, a record of polls, comparisons with previous elections, anti statistical analyses, with index of constituencies and candidates. It will be seen, therefore, that the volume is au,exceedingly useful one for reference purposes. The weak i spots n the town 1 and in tine government of the town are freely exposed, and suggestions, -More or less practical; are made with a Viewto improvement. The writers are agreed in dwell- infon the lack of public spirit on the part of the mem- bers of theCorPoration ; and it would be well if som'e of those who take part in the managenlent of local affairs woulctread these stringent criticisms upon their conduct. The" English .Illustrated Magazine" (price 6d.) is distinguished this month by a frontispiece which is a splendid portrait of Mr. Gladstone, engraved by W. Biscombe Gardner from a photograph by Mr. S. A. Walker, of Regent-it., London. The portrait cer- tainly deserves to rank as one Of the finest, if not absolutely the finest, which has ever been issued. div.head: DEATH OF THE EARL OF ESSEX.
div.p: DEATH OF THE EARL OF ESSEX.

The death of the Earl of Essex, took place on Sunday, at Cassiobury Park Watford, at the great age of eighty- nine years. By his first marriage Lord Essex had three sons, the eldest of whom, Arthur de Vere Viscount Malden, married, in 1853,Emma Martha, third daughter of the late Sir Henry Meux, Bart., and died in 1879, leaving two sons, Lard Capell and the hon. Randolph de Vere Capell, and several daughters. The Earl of Essex resumed, by 'Royal licence in 1380, the ancient ortho- graphy of his family name Capell in lieu of Capel. Lord Capell succeeds his grandfather in the titles and estates. FRIGHTFUL RAILWAY COLLISION iN AMERICA. '8 KILLED AND 25 INJURED.

A railway collision, in which eigt&L persons were killed and twenty-five others injured, occurred on Saturday night, at Watertown Junction, near Boston. A train crowded with passengers,as is usual on Saturday nights, had arrived at the junction, and was stopping on the main line, previous to crossing the main leading to the Watertown branch line, when a goods train suddenly approached and crushed into the rear of the passenger train, shattering it to pieces, and jamming the occup- ants beneath the debris. Such was the force of the collision that the front end of the boiler and cylinder of the engine of the goods train were smashed,the escaping steam adding to the horror of the situation. A passenger in the car next the rear one gave the following account of his experience :—I was dosing on the seat, and was thrown violently to the floor by the shock. Nearly every other person in the car was also thrown down. Two men and a boy jumped from the , rear end of the car, and were the only persons therein who were not more or less bruised. OF course the rear car suffered the most. The engine of the other train ploughed through it, splittine it in two, and carrying death in its path. The shrieks and cries of the injured were terrible. The dead and the injured lay in every direction. Those still alive were conveyed to the hospital as quickly as possible. The passengers in the other four cars were all terribly shaken.

div.head: DISPUTE BETWEEN CORONERS.
div.p: A DISPUTE BETWEEN CORONERS.

On Sunday morning an old man named Patrick Flyna was found lying dead at the bottom of the stairs of his house in Knutsford-rd., Latchford. Flynn was a tanner's labourer, and it is stated that on Saturday afternoon he was drinking heavily About 7 o'clock he was put to bed and his wife and son remained in the kitchen all night. The son on awaking on Sunday morning found his father lying at the bottom of the stairs apparently dead. Dr. Ronald was sent for, and on his arrival he said deceased had been dead several hours, hav- ing troken his neck. In the usual way the Warrington p.lice communicated the occurrence to Mr. Yates' of Macclesfield, who, as coroner, has been in the habit of holding inquests in that part of Warrington which lies on the Cheshire side of the river. Mr. Yates, however, replied that he had been advised by the clerk to the Cheshire County Council that Warrington, since the passing of the Local Government Act, 1888, was considered to be wholly in the county of Lancashire, and although Latchford is on the Cheshire side of the river Mersey, it fornied part of the borough, and was thus beyond his jurisdiction. The police at once communicated this information to Air. Brighouse, coroner for South-West Lancashire, and lie, in reply, wired that he had no jurisdiction in Latchford, anct therefore could not hold the inquest. Mr. Yates was again communicated with on Monday night, con- veying Mr. Brighouse's reply. The matter was brought to the notice of the borough town-clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle) on Tuesday morning, and he wrote the Home Secretary explaining circumstances. Meantime the deceased's body was removed to the mortuary to await the inquest.

div.head: MR. BRIGHOUSE INTERVIEWED.
div.p: MR. BRIGHOUSE INTERVIEWED.

On Tuesday night Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner for Lan- cashire, was at St. Helens, where is attention was drawn to the statement made that a difference had arisen between himself and Mr. Yates, the coroner for Cheshire, relative to the holding of inquests in Latchford, a por- tion of the borough of Warrington. situate in the county of Chester. ' Mr. Brighouse very courteously consented to give some details of the subject in dispute, and in reply to questions said:-4 report of the death of Flynn was forwarded to my office at Orinskirk by the Chief Constable of Warrington, together with a telegram he (the Chief Constable) had received from Mr. Yates. I communicated by telegram with the Chief Constable .(Mr. Hunt), to the effect that I had jurisdiction in the county of Lancaster, but that I knew of nothing that gave sue jurisdiction outside that county, • Who has held inquests up to now in Latchford Mr. Btighouse ,: So far Mr. Yates has held inquests in that part of the borough of Warrington which lies in Cheshire, and 1 wired to tho Chief Constable of War- rington that the report must again be forwarded to Mr. Yates, with.an IntimatiOn that 4 Sonsidered I bad no jurisdiction. I afterwaros Wrote id MP, iittUt confirm- ing the telegram, and further pointing out that AIL Yates had held inquests in Latchford since the passing of the Local Government Bill without complaint. This is an unfortunate time to settle a point of juris- diction, is it not, Mr. Brighouse? The Conner: I have pointed out that this is a very inopportune time to raise the question—a time when a body is awaiting burial. I have suggested that Mr. Yates hold the inquest in this case, and then afterwards the question of jurisdiction can be discussed. , Have you communicated with any authority upon the matter of the jurisdiction of a coroner in another County Mr. BrighoUSe : I at once sent a copy of the telegrams and correspondence to Mr. F. C. Hutton, clerk of the peace for Lancashire and clerk to the County of 'Lan- caster, asking his 'advice, but ma to this time I kayo not received a.reply.
Over what -area do you consider your jurisdiction extends?

Mr. Brighouse: I can hold inquests anywhere in Lan- cashire, although I am allotted to the West Derby Divi- sion. When there was a vacancy in Liverpool I held inquests until the vacancy was filled, and I could hold inquests in any Lancashire town if I was requested; but beyond the couaty of Lancaster I hold I have no jurisdiction.

div.head: INQUEST.
div.p: THE INQUEST.

An inquest was held on the deceasei at the Cheshire Cheese Inn, Latchford, on Thursday afternoon, by Mr. Coroner S. Brighouse.—Mary Flynn, the deceased's wife, and Patrick Flynn, her son, gave evidence which brought out facts already stated. The deceased, the woman stated, was 62 years of age.—Patrick said he found the deceased lying at the bottom of the stairs, about ten minutes to four on Sunday morning, dead. Witness was going up to bed, and kicked the deceased's hand in the dark. •He gave an alarm to his mother. The deceased was accustomed to take too much drink at times.—MichaerWelsby deposed to being called into the house about five • Minutes past four, and finding John Flynn dead on the sofa, where he had been placed.— The jury immediately returned a verdict of" Accidental death.'

FURTHER EXPLANATION BY THE CORONER. The Coroner said perhaps the jury would not think'it out of place if he occupied a few minutes in explaining why he was there that day. He was there simply to prevent a scandal, and not because he thought he had any legal right to come amongst them, although, of course, he had no objection to come amongst a Cheshire jury, for Cheshire juries had a very good reputation in his county. Still looking at the matter in its purely legal aspect, he was satisfied that he had DO legal right to come there, and at the present moment he was a trespasser on somebody else's domain. He expressed the opinion that the Local Government Act of 1888, justified his action, though on this Act, he said, the Cheshire Coroner relied, and he repeated the statement of the circumstances previously given by him as a above. If Mr. Yate's argument was sound it must, he said, be admitted on all hands that for the last tour years he had been taking inquests that he himself ought to have taken, and thus acting illegaily. The time for raising this objection when a body was lying dead,was very inoppprtune.—(The jury in chorus : Hear, hear.)—lf the clerk to the Cheshire County Coun- cil held the opinion he did there was nothing to prevent the Cheshire coroner communicating with his brother coroner in Lancashire, and the clerk to the Cheshire County Council with the clerk to the Lancashire County Council, so that they could have read the section of the Act, discussed that matter, and, as decent folk generally did, come to some right conclusion. The clerk to the Cheshire County Council communicated with the cleric to the Lancashire County Council, who, he was sorry to say, was away on his holidays, so that the matter came under the cognizance of a deputy. He felt persuaded in his mind that the deputy had not sufficiently considered the Act of Parliament, and he felt that at the present time he was not before the jury legally, and he could assert that he had simply come there to prevent public scandal. (The jury: Hear hear). If after reflection and consideration of the Act of Parliament it did come about that the concensus of opinion was that he should come there,they could rest assured that he should not come un- willingly. He should come there and do his duty with the assistance of the gentlemen of his juries in Cheshire. (The jury : Hear hear.) But until it was so decided he thought he had a right to complain. The Act of Parliament he referred to said :—"A place which is part of an adminis- trative county for the purposes of this Act shall, subject as in this Act mentioned,form part of that county for all purposes, whether sheriff, lieutenant, custos rot closure, justice, militia, coroner, or other." If that section was to be studied by itsel, he should quite think that Latch- ford being a part of the county of Lancashire for ad- ministrative purposes, he ought to have held the inquests there. But the section had a proviso attached to it, for in a sub-section it was provided :—" This enactment shall net affect the existing powers or privileges of any city or borough as respects the sheriff, lieutenant,militia, justice, or coroner, but if any county borough is at the passing of this Act a part of any county for any of the above-named purposes, nothing in this Act shall prevent the same from continuing to be part of that county for that purpose." It seemed very plain that the enactment should not affect the existing powers in the borough, and • before the Act was paQsed the existing powers were that the Cheshire coroner had to come to Latchford. At any rate, the question would be thrashed out in detail. He did not want to make his first appearance in the county of ICheshire under false pretences. There was one point which was rather a humorous phase of the subject, but still you ought perhaps to end your story with sons e humour. When his salary was revised, last January but one, it was revised on the assumption that he should not hold an inquest in that part of the borough, and when Mr. Yate's salary was revised, he felt sure it was revised on the assumpiion that he should hold inquests there. (Laughter.)—A Juror : You will have to bring Mr. Ya'es in as a trespasser.—The foreman, Mr. Thos. Ireland, said the jury were very pleased to hear the explanation. It had put matters in the proper light, and he was sure it was very kind of Mr.' Brighouse to come and hold the inquest, under the circumstances. 11 They were all sorry it had been delayed so lonz, still it was better that it had not ' been delayed longer.— rho Coroner: I can only say that if it does come about that I have to come amongst you I feet I shall have very great service and aid from you. The funeral left the deceased's residence, close by. immediately after the inquest, the coffin being covered with wreaths contributed by relatives and friends.

div.head: lONIE 5
div.p: lONIE 5
-THE PRIDE OF THE MILL
A THRILLING LOVE STOR7 Bit LAURA JEAN LIBBEY
CHAPTER XIII.
"I REALLY BELIEVE THAT A SPECIAL PROVI- DENCE BRINGS ABOUT THE MEETING OF THIS TWO WHO ARE DESTINED TO LOVE FACE
OTHER," SHE SAID,

Colonel Whitney made no concealment of his satfsfaction and approval when Arthur Rochester called upon his 3, the next day, and informed him ,his betrothal to lonie, adding, all that they needed now to make them happy was his consent. "And that you certainly have, my boy," declared the colonel, heartily. "I am more than satisfied with her choice. If there is one thing that is commendable in a young girl, it is to see her marry for love."

"It is my one sorrow that I will not be able to surround my darling with luxury," said Arthur, with a sigh; "but, depend upon it, I shall work all the harder. The love of a fair young girl, and looking forward to a happy future, give new zest,to a man's work."
"I suppose so," returned Colonel Whitney; the confirmed bachelor looking into the fire with an audible sigh. _ .

For a week—a short week—the lovers lived in a paradise of their own; in their after lives—lives of sorrow and bitterest pain—they boils liked to look back at it, and remember it. At the end of the week business in the interest of the firm took Arthur Rochester to Philadelphia. "I am to be gone a fcrtnight at least, my darl- ing," he said; "and when I return I am going to claim you at once. Delays are dangerous, you know."

Tonle protested that she couldn't think of wed- ding so soon. Why, there was a trousseau to be pre- pared, and— He interrupted her with a kiss. 4 "Remember you are going to be a poor man's bride, dattag," be said. "Let us have no fess, no ceremony. I cannot wait the length of time that ft would take to get all those thins ready. Make we happy by promising me thi t our marriage shall take place just a 9 soon as I /*dual."
, He looked so eager, so handorne, his batl,B Were clinging to hers, his beseeching eyes were seaVhing her face so wistfully, how could she refuse v:ilen she loved hlin.so

lonie prom iied at length, and he left her, the happiest of men, little dream ng—Heaven help him f—under what pitiful circumstances they were id meet again. It seemed an age to bole until his first letter came. She would not break the seal and look over its contents before the cola eyes of another. She took it to her own room, and sat down by the window in the sunshine with it, wondering, in delletful suspense, what was written 1'40.* tbat seared envelope. The beautiful face dimpled and flushed as she read his letter through. The letter would have satisfied even the most loving and sensitive heart. He told her how he loved her, how long the days seemed away from her, how he missed her, and that the world seemed empty because she was not near him, and bow true he meant to be to her—forever and forever. How she kissed the words as she read them, as women do the written words of the mea they love. Each day the mail brought her a letter from him, and in the last he said : _ .

"I shall be back three days from now, lonie. You may expect to see me just as soon as I can be driven from the depot to the villa. I shall hope that you will be on the porch to greet me. I am afraid I shall not be able to write much more, my time will be filled so completely." "Three days more and he will return to me," she murmured, with tear-wet eyes. "Oh, was there ever a happier girl than I?" The ticking of the gilded clock on the marble mantel seemed to say: Arthur is coming home." That was the song the birds swinging in their cages in the sunshine seemed to warble: "Arthur is com- ing home." Even the wind that stirred the ivy leaves outside of her window seemed to whisper to her beating heart: "Arthur is coming home.' She was so wrapped up in her own bright golden day dreams that she failed to notice the awful change that had come over the colonel, and which dated exactly a week back. On that night he had staggered into the house a little before midnight as ghastly pale as he would ever be when he was lying in a coffin, dead. None of the servants had seen him. He had opened the door cautiously with his latch-key, and groped his way up to his own room like a man stricken blind. The next afternoon Frank Lyons called, and, to the servant's surprise, inquired for the colonel in- stead of Miss lonie.

They were closeted together for over two hours, and when Mr. Lyons took his leave there was a smile so evil on his dark, handsome face that Jen- kins, the butler, could have annihilated him for it. Aud shortly after this there was a sharp peal from their master's bell

Jenkins," he said, when the man hastened to answer the summons, "bring me a glass of brandy —strong." "Are you ill, sir?" cried the man, in alarm, when he saw the colonel's ghastly face. "Make haste," replied the colonel, turning ab- ruptly away. "I am passing through the bitter- ness of death. Heaven save me from going mad." The colonel did not leave his room that day. He took no food—no nourishment other than that glass of brandy which he had drained at a single draught. All that night he paced up and down the floor of his room, like a man distracted. At last Jenkins made bold to go to the door during the night, and ask his master if there was anything he could do for him.

"The greatest kindness you can do me is to leave me alone," he groaned. By the greatest effort he controlled himself to .go down to the table the next morning. His morning paper lay beside his plate, and a vase of cut flowers stood on the table. lie pushed the paper from him; he could not read ; the letters would dance before his gaze in words of scorching, burning fire. He could not eat; food would choke him.

lonie came tripping into the breakfast-room as dainty, as fresh and sweet as a flower. It was strange she did not notice the colonel's wonderful agitation as she kissed him, and bade him a merry " good morning, uncle." As we have said,, a week passed, and each day the colonel's agitation increased, though he strove man- fully to conceal it from lonie. On the morning she received Arthur's last letter, after she had read it, she hurried at once to the library, where she was sure she would find the colonel. Yes, he was there sitting by his desk, his face buried in his hands.

lonie stole up behind him, and the next instant two soft white arms stole around his neck, and a sweet, dimpled cheek was pressed close to his. " lonie, my dear, is it you ?" he said huskily. "Yes, uncle," she answered, cheerfully. "I have come to tell you what Arthur said in his last letter. He is coming home, uncle, in three days. Three days must pass somehow. Then he will be with us again." "And you are happy over it, dear ?" he asked, feverishly. "Of course, uncle," she said, shyly; and a lovely flush like the crimson heart of a wild rose surged from her neck to her dainty brow. He suppressed the bitter groan that rose to his lips. "Are not you, uncle ?" she asked, wonderingly; adding, with just the slightest suspicion of girlish pique: "Why do you not say you are glad, too, that he will be with us so soon 7 You like Arthur, don't you, uncle?" "Yes, yes, child," he said, huskily. "Why shouldn't 1 7"

- - "YOU should, of course, uncle? And the clasp of the white arms tightened about his neck. "Are you very happy over your coming marriage, lonic 7" he asked, wistfully. "Sit down on this hassock at my feet, and tell me about it. It will be a great comfort to me to ponder over your words." The conversation did net strike her then as being at all strange; but she looked back at it in the dark after-days, and wondered how she could ever have been so blind as not to have known that there was something terribly wrong. "You want me to tell you how happy I am ?" she answered, with a delightful, girlish laugh. " Why, I hardly know how to begin—how to answer you, uncle." "You love Arthur Rochester with all your heart, do you net, lonie I" he asked, huskily and eagerly —oh! very eagerly. "I do, or I should never have consented to be his wife," answered the girl, proudly, the long lashes drooping bashfully over the lovely dark, velvety eyes. "You might have learned to love some one else in

"I hardly know 170-w to begin, lonie," he said, huskily, "but I suppose it is the better way to break into the subject at once." "Yes, that is the best way, uncle," she agreed. He laid one trembling hand on the dark, curly head, looking wistfully down into those beautiful dark eyes. "You have promised to trust me—to believe in me," he said, solemnly, "no matter what comes, no matter,how great the shock." " I shall always believe in you, uncle," she replied, just as 'solemnly. "My affection is as true as steel—as faithful as the unswerving magnet to the pole." Crushing back the great lump that rose in his throat, Colonel Whitney went on slowly: "My terrible trouble dates back just one week ago to-day, lonie. You recollect I did not come home until midnight. I—l dined in the city that evening." "Yes, I remember, uncle," she answered, with a blush; for I remember I waited so late for you. I wanted to show you a letter from Arthur, where —where he wrote that he had made arrangements with a clergyman that he knew to—to perform the ceremony that was to make his sweetheart his little wife." _ . _

And she hid her pretty, blushing, dimpled face on her uncle's arm with a merry, girlish laugh. Heaven help her, it was the last joyous, mirthful laugh that would fall from those red lips for full many a year; for a woman's heritage of bitter sor- row was to fall over her, shutting her out front love and happiness for evermore. (To be continued).

TILE REVI SIN G BARRISTER AT W A RRINGTON. SATURDAY. Mr. James Thomas Foard, revising barrister, eontinued his revision of the lists of voters Lit -the Town Hall, on Saturday. Mr. William ZlnYtOn, Liberal registration agent, and Mr. A. zrowne again appeared to represent the Liberal interest, and Mr. Hampson, Conservative agent, to represent the Conservatives. There was a large attendance of claimants. THREE CLAIMS FOR ONH TENEMENT. Three occupation claims for the mu...cipal franchise Were advanced on behalf of Margaret Lythgoe, widow, and her daughters, Margaret Lythgoe, and Eliza- iseth Lythgoe, in respect to a shop and dwelling-house, the premises being situated at 35, Sankey-st.—Mr. nanapson supported and Mr. Browne opposed the appli- lation.—Mr. Browne said the widow was only a tenant , the house by devise, and there was no separate en- , trance to the house, hut it had to be entered through , The shop, consequently there was no separate occupation 'ef the house.—Mr. Sampson said the claimants had been tenants long enough to claim, although there was succession by devise. Mere Was an entrance to the house by a back teev.—Mr. Browne said that was not the case.—The na„ rrister :I shall want some proof that there are rooms ler living so as to form a dwelling-house.--Mr. Hamp- , lon : They have a room as well as a shop.—Mr. Browne: eh it is ridiculous. There are the mother and three ~,,ilaughters living together. It is only a bedroom for "iem.—His Honour : The mother is entitled for the dwelling-house as the owner.—Mr. Browne: No, sir, it is only for her life. It belongs to trustees.—The „ Revising Barrister: At any rate, she has the •ecupation franchise.—Mr. Browne: Oh, not long ell„. °ugh, sir; it is only about eight months since Mr. !,./thgoe diet —The Barrister said it was vested in censtees. and she was the beneficiary owner.—Mr. Hanapson : It is in trust for herself.—Mr. Browne ; For her life, and her daughters after.—llis Honour said he lid not think Mr. thunpson, with all his ingenuity, could get three votes out of the premises. If he would bring Proof that there was any structural severance of the ?use from the shop he might be prepared to consider Lae ease, but the house and shop appeared to be all one. ula allowed the claim of Margaret Lythgoe, sen., in respect to the dwellingpouse, but disallowed the other slams.

Quatavrxxo IN JAIL. Charles Fudge, a working man, claimed in respect of a , 'IOUS() HI Green's Contr.—Mr. Browne supported, and kr. 'lampoon opposed the claim. Mr. Hampson asked 111., e claimant whether he had not been committed to lail during the qualifying period for assaulting his wife. , --He replied in a very demonstrative fashion, that he WaS sent to jail, but not for felony or assaulting his ' !Ye, but for spending his own money for a drop of adding in a loud voice "That is nowt." (Laugh- , "Ir.) His Honour : You must not come here to make Yclurself a buffoon because they do that at the circuses. ; The claimant : Yes. I know they do.—The Barrister : ' You have been in prison. That is a fatal objection.— ; Mr. Hampson said his ajection was that the claimant 4.,341 been residing at more than the prescribed distance miles, namely at Walton.—Mr. Browne : Strangeways. (Laughter.)—His Honour said Mr. Hampson had rather a queer way of putting it. He did not know whether Mr. ',lampoon was given to joking; but this seemed Itore than a joke. (Laughter.)—Mr. Browne : It might loft said that he is disqualified on the ground that he had not occupied, but it could not be said that a man resided in a jail. Surely that objection is bad.—The Barrister said the objection was good enough for the pur- Dose. it was clear that the man had been compulsorily I, Siding somewhere for the benefit of his country. (Laughter.) His Honour disallowed the claim.—The ''ltirtiant asked to be allowed his day's expenses.—His Honour: No, nothing, you lase your vote. "AIM BY MESSRS. SEEITON.—A. LIMITED COMPANY AND THEIR HEHISTERED OFFICE. I,MR. W. P. Skelton applied that himself and his brother ,_r.W. Skelton might be placed on the list with respect Premises in Horsemarket-st.—Mr. Hammon sup- _vurted, and Mr. Browne opposed the application.—ln rPIY to Mr. Browne the claimant said the concern was 'egistered in March as a limited company, but the corn- libt,atly had not yet take.' possession of the premises.—Mr. -"rowne And yet the word limited is up over the door, nd the words " registered office" of the company on a rass plate, and then you say they havent taken pos- •oseion.—The Claimant: I say they have not taken pos- "eau jou of either ti., business or the premises.—Mr. "roWne Although it has been registered five months, at.41)111 yoa have put over your door "W. P. and W. Skel- „; Limited." Is the registered office of the company 'uere P—The Claimant: The registered office of the corn- is there.—Mr. Browne: In what name are the Pretnises rated P—The Claimant: The prospectus has 11°t been issued yet.—Mr. Browne said this was an !?ttraordinary case. Here were some gentlemen turning ..,11eir business into a litnited company and putting the ~words .• limited "and registered "office over the door °c`ficl nobody could tell who was the conipany.—The _iaimant : Simrtly because it is compulsory to put that un from the date the register.—His Honour said the tl.llPany might have a registered office there without ,Vng tenants. The company had no actual existence at present moment. He allowed the claim. AN ILLITERATE VOTER INDEED' man whose name was called out as 'Thomas Ctin- Cie, 23, Back Cottages hail an objection made against b!n by the Conservalive side. the work is generally well advanced. It is at this place that the deepest cutting on the whole line of the canal has had to be made in consequence of the'', being a rise in the ground. From the top of the canal bank to the bottom of the canal, the depth is nearly seventy yards, and when vessels sail along the 26 feet of water they will be hidden from view by the tremendously high banks. A little above Old Quay Docks, a bridge has had to be cunstructed. for the convenience of the work- men at the Chemical Works on the other iide, and the finishing touches are beings nit to it. It is a swing bridge worked by 4ydraulic power which is obtained from a high water tower erected on the spot. There is also constructed a watch tower for the man who will have to control the Bridge, and he will have within view a fine stretch of the canal to Runcorn Bridge,:and a considerable distance in the other direction. It may be mentioned that the canal at this point is somewhat narrower than the average width of the canal, in consequence of the Bridge. Lower down it may be noticed that

centuries, and which in the near future will he covered again. The river wall from the Old Quay to No Man's Land is completed, and one important piece of work for Widnes traders is practicully completed. That is

THE WIDNES LOCK which is intended for the transfer of the vessels and flats from Widnes Docks to the canal. The Lock is of large dimensions. being 395 feet long, and 45 feet wide. At the time of my visit, men were employed in hanging the huge gates, and were fixing on the walls the.mooring stumps, or what are commonly called mushroom's. The gates are made of green-heart, which is one of the hardest and toughest woods known. With the exception of a month or two, three years have been consumed in making the lock, and considering the natute of the the work and the conditions under which it has had to be pertormed, it cannot be held to be otherwise than an expeditious piece of engineering.

No MAN'S LAND AND CASTLE ROCK, the site of Runcorn's ancient castle when Queen Ethelfleda ruled the land, have disappeared,and the topographical guide to Runcorn in the future will not mention that historical spot. There are in existence a few prints which depict the river and the Runcorn foreshore as it was before the railwAy bridge was built, and in which Castle Reck is de- picted, and one would think that these would become valuable in the market now. The gunn- ing away of the rock has been successfully carried on, and the resident engineer will soon be able to

niniCoas DOMES are quickly reached, and a forsaken appearance thiey present. With the exceptio,n of a flat or two, there is not a vessel to be seen, whereas previously schooners, barges, and fiats have been present in scores. The closing of these docks has been a very sore point indeed to the traders of the port, but they have to endure what now cannot be cured, albeit they use an Englishman's privage to Fum- ble very freely. The trade is being dealt with at IVeston Point, and Weaver Pool; and the Ship Canal Company offer traders and the seamen the conveni- ence of a steamer which runs twice a day to and from Weston Point and Weaver Pool. But the best that can be devised is far from being equal to the arrangements and conveniences that existed when the dock& were open, audit is most devoutly wished on all hands that they may be opened at the prom- ised time, which I heard was March. A brief walk along the river's aids brings into view the cause of what cannot be said to be less than a calamity to the town. This is the REMNANTS OF BRIDGEWATER, LOCK, which were partially demolished during a storm in February last. The engineers held that they could not repair the enormous damage which was done and finish the lock unless water was shutout from the channel, and this meant the closing of Runcorn Docks. A very large staff of men is at present

The poisonous gas was almost over- whelming, and they were several times driven back by its fumes. The body of Ball was first reached, and after it had been conveyed to the bottom of the shaft the ' rescuers returnod to their self-imposed labours. An hour elapsed before the body of Sharrock was recovered, and it was not till another half hour had passed that the body of Cook was brought to the pit" eye." The relief party have been generally complimented up•as their brave conduct.

of the canal a large shed is in course of erection for the purpose of storing china clay and other pottery material, and good progress is being made with the construction of jetties for the loading and unload- ing of ships. But with present arrangements much despatch has been displayed in both the loading and unloading of ships, as paragraphs previously pub- lished in this journal will show. In conclusion it may be said that the work in Runcorn district is progressing very satisfactorily, and if there be an absence of mishaps we may have the Ship Canal in operation sooner than those people imagine who are apt to take a gloomy view of things.

of tile low price of ammonia liquor, Mr. Carr advised the Committee to put up a plant to manufac- ture sulphate of ammonia, and his suggestion was car- ried out, with the result that last year if they had sold the ammonia liquor it would have yielded about £503 or £6OO ; whereas the sulphate of ammonia yielded about £1,700. The quality of the gas had been im- proved by extending the ppurifying plant, and the gas now sold was of very good quality. In 1882 the gas works were capable of producing 560,000 cubic feet per day ; now they were capable of producing a million cubic feet per day. In Mr. Carr they had one of the best managers there was in the country. The same re- marks would apply very largely in regard to the Water Works. In 1882 they pumped 527 million gallons, for • which they received about £ll,OOO. In 1892, they pumped 957 million gallons for which they received £14,000. Mr. Brown described the alterations and improvements that Mr. Carr had intro- duced into the engines and pumping machinery. In 1882 they were capable of pumping 1,800,000 gallons per day. While now they could pump nearly 3 millions and when the new works were completed at Netherley in the course of a week or two they would be able to pump 5 million gallons per day. And the new works, capable of punaping 2i million gallons per day would be built and completed for the small outlay of £9,000. These were all points attributable to good management. It would be presumptive on his part to say that all was due to Mr. Carr. There was a great deal due to the management. It was to the Chairman and others who first conceived and carried out the idea that Widnes should posse,s the gas and 'water works and who laid down the lines on which the works should be carried on, but Mr. Gossage must confess that there was many a well organised scheme spoiled by bad management and by want of attention. The Corporation would come into a most niagnificient property. If they in Widnes charged the same price for the gas and water as was charged in neighbouring towns the prefits would be enormous, but the policy of the Board had been to fester the true interests of Widnes, which he hoped would be main- tained a centre where manufacturers would be able to manufacture at a cheaper rate than other towns. (Hear, hear.) He was quite happy to leave the matter in the hands of the Board.—Mr. Taylor seconded the motion.—Mr. Beech argued that the matter had been sprung on the B iard and that it was arranged the matter should not be brought fcrwards until the new, works at Netherly were completede; He could not see the sense of attempting to raise an officials salary at the present time when in two months he would have to be re-appointed by the Council. There was no doubt they had been receiving great profits from gas ; lent had it been gas. Until lately it/had not been up to the mark, by a great deak He had nothing to say about Mr. Carr and hie abilities ; he was quite satisfied with his work, but this was an inopportune time to deal with salaries and he moved that the minute be rejected.—Mr. Tilley seconded tbe motion.—Mr. Heyes said Mr. Brown's,facts proved that Mr. Carr was worth the money, and he would get it elsewhere. (Mr. Beech: Let him try). If the gas and water undertaking were in the hands of a private com- pany, his salary would be a great deal more. The pro- posal was reasonable and modest.—Mr. Neil said if he • were to speak the feelings of the outside public, he should vote against the increase, but if the public had no con- fidence in them they would not send them to the Board. They had a better knowledge of Mr Care's abilities and how the money was being spent than the public could have; if they had not they had no busin -as there. Alter considering all the details he had come to the conclueion that it was a reasonable increase , and he should vote in favour. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Owens said he should not attempt to make an electioneering speech. There was a great deal said about the rights of worlong-men, and he believed in justice to the working-man. He believed in justice to every man and a skilled mm' should be paid a skilled price. Since Mr. Carr had been manager, the reduction in the price of gas had been equavelent to the distribution of £13,000 amongst the gas consumers, which was a splendid tribute to his excellent management. Mr. Carr did not come th-re as a water engineer but his perceptive faculties end sound judgment had enabled him to make an excellent water engineer as results had proved. They were handing down" a splendid property to the Corporation ; let themn hand *down an engineer with a salary commensurate with his ability and experience. They had too grand a property to be dealt with by an inexperienced man.— Mr. Taylor said he was surprised at Mr. Beech. In committee, he was one of Mr. Cart's strongest support- ers. Mr. Beech :It is not true.—Mr. Taylor appealed to the other members it that was not so.—The Chairman said it was a mistake to talk about increasing the salar- ies for the new Corporation and so on. Tile Council when elected would consider the officers on their merits and settle their salaries.—Mr. saidwood said la had only had the figures placed in his hands ten minutes and he had not had time to consider them and should therefore not vote.—Mr. Brown in replying said Mr. Carr did not come as a professional water engineer, but he had ap- plied limseif to thestudy of that science and he was now a member of the Society of Civil Engineers. He corroborated. Mr. Taylor's statement with regard to Mr. Beech. As to the time being inopportune. He had not made an election speech, and he thought the ratepayers would judge what was done for their interest, and what was claptrap meant to secure their vot(s. He believed eincerely as the manager of a manufacturing concern, that Mr. ,Carr was exceptionally able, and consequently he sincerely in the interests of the town, recommended Mr. Cart's advance. For thc amendment, there voted Messrs. Beech and Tilley-2; against Messrs. Brown, Conk, Timmis, Owen, Heyes, Taylor, Houghton, and Neil-8. The minutes v ere • then put and carritd iinanitasously.

div.head: OPENING OF THE INQUEST.
div.p: OPENING OF THE INQUEST.

On Tuesday night, Mr. Brighouse. county coroner, opened an inquest, at the Waggon and Horses Hotel, Haydock. After the jury had been sworn, the Coroner said Gentlemen, I have only come down to-night to open this inquiry into the deaths of these three men so as to give the necessary burial orders so that the burials may take place as soon as possible. I propose, with your consent, to adjourn to another day, so that we may go into all the details in connection with these deaths. I should suggest Monday morning next at half-past nine. The jury having agreed to this course, the Coroner con- tinued :—I wish to take this opportunity of saying for myself —and I know I am saying it for you—what sym- pathy we have for all the relatives who are suff..ring by these deaths, and what a sad calamity it is. I know :I am expressing your opinions when I express my own on that subject. But we have also a legal duty to per- form, and we shall have to find out how the deaths have taken place. The coroner then said he had been in com- munication with Mr. Ellis, solicitor to Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., respecting the date and hour of the adjournment. Monday morning did not suit Mr. Ellis, but on account of many business engagements, he (the coroner) could not Rs it later than half-past nine.

..... „. Mr. Robinson, general manager of Messrs. Evans and Co.'s colleriea, said he had no doubt Monday nywning would suit all the other officials concerned. The Coroner said the Government Inspector would want to make all enquiries. Mr. Robinson said the Government Inspector had been down the pit that day. The coroner then took the evidence of identification, and the jury were bound aver to appear on Monday morn- ing, when the evidence will be gone into.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

Toe monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday. Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., presided, and there were present Messrs. B. Brown, J. Midwood, R. Cook, G. I. Neil, S. Owen, J. Beech, J. Tilley, 11. S. Timmis, F. Heyes, J. Taylor, J. Houghton, H. S. Oppenheim (law clerk), T. Craik, (assistant clerk), S. Hoyle (accountant), Dr. A. O'Keeffe (medical officer). W. Lowe (nuisance inspector.)

PROPOSED NEW POST. OFFICE. Mr. Joseph Ison, of Blackpool,appointed postmaster to Widnes, wrote stating, it had come to his knowledge that technicaf schools were about to be erected by the Widnes Local Board. The postal authorities were desirous of obtaining a new post office and it had been thought probable that tho Board might feel disposed to erect a suitable post office at the sometime, and on the same site.—The Chairman said the Board had nothing to do with the matter; the letter must have been written under a misapprehension.—The Clerk said he had replied to that effect. OAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.. .

The Gas and iVa;;G;;In-iitee—r-e-r;.-rted that accounts amounting to £767 7s. 2d. on gas account and £1,239 I ss. Od. on water account bed been examined and passed , for payment. The gas had been tested on the 19th and 29th ult., when the illuminating pJsver was 1928. ind 18.87 candles respectively. The engineer reported that the building contract for the Netherley extensiop was practically completed and the men were pushing forward 1 with the work for the contract ef the engine and pumps. Messrs. Bathorn, Davey, and Co., state that everything would be completed and ready fer starting in a fort- night's time. The mean rainfall during the month had been 3.835 inches, and the water in stock on the 310 August was 10,173,658 gallons. The illuminating power of the gas during the month had averaged 18.62 candles. The wages required for the next four weeks is for gas and water works £ll5 per week. The Committee recommended that the salary of Mr. Isaac Carr, gas and water engineer, be increased from £4OO to £5OO. INCREASE OF ENGINEER'S SALARY. In moving the adoption of the above minutes, Mr. Brown said the recommendation with regard to the engineers's salary was made purely because the Commit- tee believed it was due to his ability and work. Mr. Carr had been with the Board ten years; and in 1882 they made or sold 66,296,000 cubic feet of gas, giving a revenue of £11,385. In 1892 they sold 126,761,000 cubic feet, giving ,a revenue of £12,693. Thus while the quantity sold had increased by 90 per cent., the money received had only increased 7 per cent. The profit in 1882 was £3,145 and in 1892 £2,640. These results had not been obtained because raw material was less in price at the present time. Coal was 2s. 3d. per ton dearer than it was in 1882, and the price of residuals had fallen. In 1882 tar was £2 ss. a ton ; last year it was only 20a. The price of ammonia liquor was then 20s. per ton, last year it was only worth 6s. per ton. That they could sell so much more gas and have only about £BOO more money showed a very great improvement in, the man- agemmt of the manufacture. Mr. Carr had doubled the quantity of coke available for sale, mean- ing a sum of something like £.1,7000, purely through his skilful management. In consequence

William was not responsible for Thomas.—Mr. Browne explained that the father lived with the claimant, but to compel the other son to contribute to Isis support he applied to the magistrates, who obtained an order against this other sort to contribute.—The claim wasallowed. The latter's objection was that the applicant, his father being in a lunatic asylum, was in receipt of relief.—The applicant said his father had been in the asylum six years, during which time he had kept the house on and maintained his mother and the rest of the family at home, but had not paid to- wards his father's support in the asylum.—Mr. Ramp- son said the father had been taken to the asylum by order of the magistrates, therefore the claim was bad.— Mr. Browne argued that the claim was good, as the magistrates had made no order against the claimant for contribution to his father's maintenance.—Mr. Hampson said there did net ?eein to him to be any distinctien.— Mr. Browne : There may not be to a mind like yours.— Mr. Hampson : all minas are not so boyish as yOurs.— Mr. Browns: I don't want any impudence.—Mr. Hampson referred in support of his contention to a case of disquatification, but the Revising Barrister said that was a case in which the claimant's wife had been sent to an asylum under a magistrates' order by the Board of Guardians, and an order was made against him to 'ray for her maintenance. His Honour allowed the 1 aim.

The busihess of the 'day commenced about ;eleven o'clock.-13is Honour being an hour late through in- ability to get sooner from Southport, where he was residing—and concluded shortly before four.

The minutes of the ilea itli Commirtee contained the Surveyor's report, which steted that 677 loads of night- soil had been removed during, the month. Nine mat- tresses and three beds had been destroyed. With regard to the Infectious Diseases Hos; ital, the Surveyor states: M. attention having been called to several damp walls in the wards and house,' modes eareful examination of them and find that the brtekwork and mortar is very poromn, the i &its of the brietwork require to be raked , out and punted with cement, and the walls and stone- work coated with a darn:., proof solution'. A' the last meeting there were 8 patients in the Accident Hcßpital ; admitted since 13 ; total 19 ; parir-nts dismissod 9, died 4, 13 ; still in 6. At the inG•etious Dis roes hospital there were 6 patients at last inekting, admitted since, 6; discharged, 5 ; died, 0; still in 7. Ii was reonnnendecl that the hollowing appointnnents , 0 the liospi`al staff be approved :—lnfectious Hospital, Miss Auensta Morton, as third probationer, at a salary of £l4 firSt year, and £l6 second year with uniform.—Accident Hospital, Nurse H nehes 8A temporary nurse from Augii:t 11 to 26th, at £1 is. per week. The Medical Offit!er reported that doting August there were 114 births and 58 deaths, being at the respective rates of 45.6 and 22 4 per 1,000.

div.head: HUM MORTALITT.
div.p: HUM MORTALITT.

The report continued :—The mortality is rather high this month, but not more than in the corresponding month last year. The increase is chief!: owing to the high death rate of children under one year of age, which is 3l,and of children from one to five sears of age,which is 10 Otherwise the town continues to be very healthy The cases of fever notified come from various parts of the town, but five are reported from Elliott-w-reet. There must be something radicall wrong with this neighbour- hood, as several cases of fever have talc•na ptiee during this year and last in Elliott-street and Gi idstone-street. In al.l cases reported disinfection has been carefully attended to ley the sanitary inspec'or, and isolation also, I have carefully inspected varions parts of the town dur- ing the month. I have paid psricular attention Co the instructions received from Dr. Th, woe in regard to the precautions to be observed against cholera,. and I have daily visited districts of the town, and instructed the occupiers to use the utmost precaution in Iteepirrz their back yards clean, and everything connected with their houses in as cleanly a state as possible. The back pas- sages in various parts of the town have been at-ended to and disinfected, and, as no doubt the Surveyor will inform you, every and additional attention has been paid to the emptying of closets. In fact every precaution has been taken against the invasion of cholera, and, for my part, I have no apprehension whatever that it will appear in our town. Moreover we have as good and pure a supply of water as exists in ens' town in England and there is no danger of its being p llsted. I have to, call your attention to the insanitary condition of the backyards and closets and aslipits in Appleton,. nrany of which are against the walls of houses and one is actually facing the street near the post office. I strongly recommend that a main sewer be built from the post office to join that at Deacon-road, and that all the closets be converted into water closets. It is the only means of remedying the very insanitary state of otherwise a very pleasant village. I beg to call your attention to the , backyards between Nos. 35 . and 45, Victoria-st , which are in a dilapidated and unhealthy cenditicn I beg to call your attention to the disgraceful pool of stag- nant water in Widnes-road, which is dang,eroirs and unhealthy and requires immediate attention. I authorised the matron of the Accident Hospital to. em- ploy an additional nurse in consequence of a number of patients taken in through the deplorable accidrnt which occurred at Hutchinson's works, and which could not b. met by the resident staff. The Committee recommended that the tender of Mr. G. S. Slorcland. for the supply and fixing of two firegratesond two stoves for the heat- ing of the wards and verandahs of the Infiactious Diseases Hospital, for the sum of £6l, be accepted. Tuesday next is the day fixed for the adjourned Licensing Sessions in Warrington; and there is every liklihood that there will be a crowded court, great interest attaches to the proceedings. -ktie question is—will the full Bench confirm the decision of the Licensing Justices in granting two new licenses for two new districts to Messrs. Qreenall, Whitley, and Co., in consideration of their giving up other licenses in congested dis- tricts

It is not, as some say, a matter of course to unnfirm ; for as a matter of fact a full license was, few years ago, granted to " The Grove "Inn in the Bewsey district, but it was not confirmed. Indeed, the policy carried out for the past 30 years has been to refusejiew licenses; and if that which as refused to an existing house should be granted lur a house as yet existing on paper only, the unfairness of the proceeding will be apparent.

And so with regard to the Battersby-lane dis- trict. Mr. Bolton is in possession ;he has offered to surrender three licenses for one new full license; and if the bench in face of this give Messrs. elreenall, Whitley and Co., a monopoly of this very district, nobody need be surprised if the public (*me to the conclusion that Greenallism is all Powerful amongst the magistrates. Greenallism to of course a form of Toryism. What then of tillers' magistrates? Are any of them ready to silet aside their principles? We shall see.

One great Liberal principle is embodied in the ords Local Option, which means that the people In the districts affected should have a voice in these matters. But have the Licensing Justices consulted them? Not for a moment. They have not even asked the big brewers to produce a single jot or tittle of evidence to show that full licenses z'e needed, and that they should be given, above other people, to Messrs. Greenall Whitley and 00. What does this mean? That the people are nothing, and that the big brewers are every- thing?

It is no use putting in the plea that the trans- action will reduce the number of licenses; - ld that Greenallism, in a spirit of true Philanthropy, is giving up something. The Plea is being laughed at. The magistrates ,tare themselves scheduled, in the past, the had which are to be "given up ;" and if they °ad done their duty then, or would do it now, there would be no need for Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co. to come into Court and " higgle 4/1(1 barter" with the magistrates about the sur- . 'render of a privilege which the .magistrate d have granted and can at any time take away. Whilst Other towns are advancing in licensing matters, (there is some 'danger that Warrington will slip back. We shall know, on Tuesday, whether it is case Of progression or retrogression—of elevation or degradation. Now that Disestablishment is in the air, it would be interesting to know what is the amount of money that would have to be dealt with under bill for disendowing the Church in Wales. It Will not be easy to get at the exact sum, as, in law, the English Church in Wales is a portion of the Established Church 'of England. The total (Lanualrevenue of the Church is stated in Whit- taker's Almanac to be about £7,250,000. Under itriy scheme, Wales should come in for a consider- able slice of this big cake.

The disestahlishment of the church in Scotland Will follow closely on that of Wales. Its annual revenue is estimated at £380,000 representing at 3 per cent, a capital sum of £12,660,666. It takes Scotchinan to understand the Scotch church question; but,breadly spealring,it may be said that there are three branches of one Presbyterian faii ; and, as one member of the family is en- dowed, it is natural,that the other two should pro- test against the injustice-!:--to say nothing of those who ;are outside altogether. Such a thing as Iltliting the three branches is, of course, out of the question. Scotch men are very particular as to who is orthoilox. It was the clerk and sexton of ?ne church, was it not P who said there was only 'Sandy Macpherson" and himself who held the ttuo faith, and he sometimes had his " doots tboot Sandy." In London there has been another Mrs. Jackson ~,e'aBe—on a small scale. A gentleman named "aines who Nw:s separated from his wife sought to her back by joining her in church, and put- 'ing his arm round her waist. It is usual for join- 411g to he accomplished in church; but not whilst Other service is proceeding, and Mr. Dairies not ,4,regardaVing had regard to this, was bound over to keep ‘nr3 peace. In Mrs. Jackson's case, it will be t'elnembered that the husband waited until his ife left church; and then literally bundled her ,sinto a carriage. And yet he didn't succeed. 41'eally, the course of true love in these cases can 4cit be made to run smooth.

On Thursday afternoon, the remains of Mr. James Mines. aged 24 years, of 17, Brunswick-street, were interred in the Runcorn Cemetery. The deceased, Since coming to town six years ago, had taken an active interest in all matters connected with St. Edward's Catholic Church, arid his sudden demise is deeply re- gretted by a large circle of friends.
