THE ACCIDENT AT BANK QUAY STATION, WARRINGTON.

The Widnes woman who, whilst crossing the main line at Bank Quay Station, about a month ago, was knocked down and run over by a passen- ger train, is progressing very satisfactorily at the Warrington Infirmary, under the care of Dr. Bowdon, the house surgeon. The woman's injuries were of a very serious character. Her leg was crushed and her arm broken, as also were several of her ribs. For a long time she lay in a very criti- sal condition, and on more than one occasion her life was despaired of. Possessing a good constiu- don, coupled with careful treatment, she has now so far progressed that she will soon be able to leave the Infirmary. Cricketing Goods.—Gasmaxn, Sports' Warehouse. War- rington.

ALLEGED ASSAULT ON THE HIGHWAY AT SPEECH. At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Peter Whitfield, a labourer from Glarston,was remanded in custody on a charge of indecently assaulting a single woman named Mary Thompson, housemaid to Miss Watts of Speke Hall, near Widnes. Between seven and eight o'clock on Tuesday evening, the prisoner, it was allemsd, followed the woman along Bank-lane where he caught hold of her from behind and threw her on the ground. lie placed his hand over her mouth to prevent her screams, but some men in the neighbourhood had heard the sounds and the prisoner on setting them approach jumped over the railings and ran across the fields. He was after- Wards captured and identified, the woman having scratched his face in the scuffle. Lawn Mowers.—GARLAND. horticultural Ironmonger, War- rington.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

I was glad to notice that at the first meeting of the new Board, the Runcorn Commissioners re- appointed the Pleasure and Recreation Grounds Committee. Although they did no business during the last year—indeed it is doubtful if they even held a meeting—yet there is plenty of scape for them. If Runcorn is ever to have such places there can be no better time than the present for securing the, for the longer the delay the more expensive the luxury will become.

The Committee might at once turn their atten- tionto Runcorn lull. It is a common impression that the people who quarry for stone and other minerals should leave the surface of the ground as they found it when they commenced operations. If that is the law, it has been :extensively set at defiance in the Runcorn district. I can remember when, not many years ago, there was a charming grassy slope leading up to the " Beetle," and which was a most popular resort in summer; now, in its place, there is a very large hole of tremendous depth.

The question arises has the qrtarry proVirietor in his search for wealth, the right not only to the minerals beneath the earth, but also to the grasay surface.--the common land which has been handed down by freeholders from time immemorial. At a recent assizes, a case was heard which would tend to show that the quarry proprietor can take no- thing more than the Lord of the Manor can give him, and that ia the minerals underneath the sur- face. In the case quoted a gentleman named William Price was tile owner of certain land in Pwllgwyn, in the county of Plint,, but there was a reservation of all mines, minerals, and quarries,wi th the usual and customary rights to Lard Moatyn. In 1881, a person named Lester obtained permission from Loa! Mostyn to obtain marl by tunnelling under the land. 11e obtained about 150 tons, and also obtained marl from adjacent land held by Major Hooks under a similar title. Major Rooks threatened action, and the work was stopped on his land.

At the end, of 1882, the defendant Company, Manger and C-1., began digging un the surface of the land which was granted to Pierce, and caused considerable damage. The plaintiff claimed that he MIS entitled to the undisturbed 'possesion of the surface of his freehold land. The defendant's coun- sel admitted that they would have to pay some damages for the disturbance of the plaintiff's land, and eventuilly the judge granted damages of £175, with costa. Here is one freeholder securing dam- ages for the disturbance of his land, and what one can do surely many can do if they will combine. It ought, therefore, to be one of the objects of our Pleasure and Recreation Grounds Committee to secure the combination of the freeholders, and Lake such steps as will restore to the people the use of ituncurn Hill, the praises of which have been so ably sung in the past. At. present Oose who fre- quent it do so at the imminent risk of life and

Another Cammittee reappointed was the Baths Committee, and we are promised that some ac- tion shall be taken this year. The desirability and necessity of baths appears to have become wholly subsidiary to that of cost, and if the same principle were applied throughout the Board's, busi- ness the town would soon honoree a wreck. Let the Committee present some feasible scheme, and the :rain Would then lie upon the Board of saying yes or no. It is not probable that baths, considering the revenue that w)uld be derived, would increase the rate more than id. or in tire X. The question to be decided is, are baths worth that expenditure?

It has been extensively believed that the Runcorn Musical Society was in a moribund condition, but it appears likely to turn out a case of suspended animation. I understand that since the last meet- ing of members, the Committee have not been idle, and that in the course of a .few days they will be able to submit recommendations which if accepted, will ensure to the society a vigorous and prosperous existence, and enable it to continue to bless the town with good mu-ic.

Next month Wplnes will be in the " throes" of one of the most exciting. School Board contests it has seen for the past ten years. The various sec- tions of those taking an active part in education are preparing for the fray. The Widnes Educational Association, wlqich advocates undenominatienal education,lias adopted three gentlemen to champion Its cause, viz., Messrs. It ibert Shaw, B. Brown and D. Lewis. It is probable that the Catholic potty will again nominate the present membei s—Dean Finegan, Father Clarke, Dr. O'Keeffe, and Mr. S. Quinn, and two others, one of whom will take the place of Dr. McDonnell. As to the action of the Church party much doubt exists. One thing I am assured is certain, and that is that Mr. T. Sutton TilloMiS *4l not again seek re- election. A deputation had been arranged this week to wait upon Mr. Timmis, with the object of urging him to continue those services which have been so fruitful of benefit to the town in the past, but Mr. TiMMid, hearing of this, wrote stating that it would be a useless errand to wait upon him, as ' his decision was irrevocable. There is a rumour that Mr. Deacon does not intend to allow himself to be nominated, but this wants confirmation and it is 'tà he hoped it is not true. Tee loss of two such independent fearless advocates of popular educa- tion would be an irreparable loss. Major Wareing and Mr. Barlow. it is expected, ' will consent to stand again. Mr. R. H. Davies in consequence of his ill-health will make his exit with the good wishes of all.

There is never a Cloud without a silver lining, we are told, and the dark cloud cast over many homes by the late lamentable accident at Hutchinson's works, has been brightened by the kindness and generosity displayed to the widows and fatherless. As the result of two benefit performances., Mr. Jas. Kiddie, the lessee of the Alexandra Theatre, gener- ' ously handed over £5O to the Accident Fund Com- mittee for distribution, and the money was equally divided amongst the sufferers. The aistrict mana- ager of the United Alkali Co. (Mr. J. Morrison), has allowed the injured men theirjull wages since the accident,less any sick money they may have drawn, and he has handed to Mr. Kelly, the father of one of the victims, a draft on the Bank of Ireland as compensation for the loss of his son. The amount has not yet transpired. He is also making arrange- ments, it is understood, to compensate the widows for the loss of their husbands.

The case of Mrs. Routledge is pointed out as a very hard one. Mr. F. Cane, the hon. sec, of the Accident Committee, who has worked most unsel- fishly and zealously for the aid of those in need, describes her as a woman in delicate health, bur- dened with seven children, only two of whom are able to earn a mere trifle. Re suggests that a few influential gentlemen should form themselves into a committee with the object of raising a public subscription, to set her up in some business or to purchase' her a small annuity, and he would be glad to receive the names of those-willing to help.
PROPOSED TRIENNIAL ELECTION OF
GUARDIANS IN RUNCORN UNION.

Next week the ratepayers in the Runcorn Union will be called upon to decide whether they will retain the present system pf electing their repre- sentatives on the Board oi Guardiane annually, or whether they will make a change, and elect their 'guardians for a period of three years. The voting papers will be distributed on. Thursday next, the 122nd inst., collected next day, and counted at Dutton Workhouse on Saturday. The Committee appointed by the Board to consider the question reported unanimously in favour of triennial elec- tions, and they have issued a handbill in which they support their view by stating that triennial elec- tions will be economical. They point out that dur- ing the past ten years elections of Guardians have cost the ratepayers the sum of .£560 ss. Mi. or an average of £56 18s. 11d. "In the event of the three years' system being adopted it is ex- pected that about £ll5 will be saved every thrOe years, and as the cost of contested elec- tiol.., increase yearly, with the incietese of population most probably a greater amount will be saved in future years:* The Commit- tee argue that a term of one year is not sufficient for a guardian to acquire the efficiency and usefulness necessary, and they point out that the members of the County Councils. School Boards and upwards of 100 Unions are elected for three years. The Committee appeal to the ratepayers to save expenditure and relieve the rates by voting in favour of triennial elections.

Mr. Brighouse held an inquest on Thursday. on the body of Peter Brownbill, aged sixty-four, a door opener in Sutton Heath Colliery, St. Helens, who, while opening a two-fold door on a steep jig brow to allow a train of waggons to pass through, was fatally crushe4. Mr. Hall, Gavettiment Inspector, said there was a certain amount of danger about- these doors, but it did not appear to have given any' of the officials the idea that it was serious. It seemed as if the deceased had not given himself suffi- cient time to open the doors. He suggested that a rope should be attached so that the man could pull the door open without leaving his refuge hole. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental Death."

div.head: REFLECTIOYI ON RAzNicut. ASYLUM.
div.p: A REFLECTIOYI ON RAzNicut. ASYLUM.

The Commissioners on Lunacy comment strongly in their report just issued upon the grievance of patients at Lancaster and Rainhill in not being able to speak to the visiting Committees. Referring to the latter asylum, they say:--" Many of the work- itig patients told us they never saw the Committee, and therefore did not speak to them. The patients feel this undoubted grievance, more especially when we tell them, as we are bound to do on appeal for discharge, that with the Committee rests the absolute power of granting them freedom. Nothing tends so much to tranquillise the patients, and therefore increase the pruspects of recovery, as lull opportunity of airing their grievances, and for this reason we hope that steps will be taken to enable each- patient to have, if desired, audience of the Committee, and an unstinted supply of paper and envelopes should be furnished to every ward."

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, six men, named Edward McCann, Nelson-street; Thomas Lofthouse, Travis-street: John Walsh, 5, Brynn- street ; John Wynne, 61, Grenfell-street ; Thonvis Whelan, 22, Wellington-street; and John Price, 33, Market-street, were charged with obtaining food by a trick, from Hatton's eating house, in Victoria- road. It appeared that on Tuesday the prisoners entered the shop and ordered six bowls of soup, which were supplied. They also partlok of potatos pie, pickles, and bread and rice pudding. Five of the men left the shop to go, saying their companion who was still at the table, would pay the " which was the extremely low one of Is. 9d. for the lot. When payment was demanded, he refused to I pay, and the police being informed, the whole of the prisoners were apprehended. The prisoners' pleaded that they were half drunk, and had the food in a joke.—Mr. H. Haskell, junr., said it was all very well to say it was a joke, but they must consider themselves very fortunate they had not been sent to the Quarter Sessions, on a more seri- ous charge. A flue of 10s. was imposed on each prisoner, or seven days in default.

DISAPPF.ARANCE OF AN OFFICIAL. Mr. Wm. Matthews, assistant sanitary inspector to the St. Helens Corporation, has disappeared under somewhat mysterious circumstances. He was the last official appointed in the sanitary de- partment, and seemed to he making satisfartory progress in the work he had taken up. On Thurs- day, the let inst., he left the office, and it is said that he was seen coming away from the football match between St -Helens and Wigan, which took place on the Knowsley-road ground the same even- ing. Since that time he has not been at the Town Hall, and all inquiries made by his family and friends have failed to discover where he has gone At a meeting of the St. Helens Health Committee on Wednesday afternoon, Dr. Robertson, assistant medical offleer. reported the disappearance of Assist- ant Nuisance Inspector Matthews since the first of September, and said there had been absolutely no trace of him. His relatives knew nothing of his whereabouts. His Corporation work had been satis- factory, whatever other reasons there might be for his disappearance. In consequence of cholera .pre- cautions and other extra work another man had been appointed temporarily to do Matthew's work. He would report at the next meeting as to the abilities of this inan.—Mr. Green thought they ought to advertise for a successor.—The Chairman (Councillor Forster) said what with smallpox at Warrington and cholera elsewhere, it was felt that something ought to be done.—Dr. Robertson said they had had thirty applications since Matthews had disappeared.—lt was decided to leave the mat- ter over until the next meeting. THE MEETING BETWEEN MASTERS AND MEN. Letters were received on Thursday by the officials of the two cotton operatives associations in Oldham asking them to join the Masters Federation in a conference on the five per cent, reduction on Tuesday in Manchester. A reply has been sent, with a request that the meeting be held on Monday, as the most favourable day for the operatives. It is believed that Monday will be ultirrii- tely fixed for the meeting..

On Tlitirsday nvirnimf there were further evidences that the run on Ow Ilicheek Bank i practically over, and that confidence has 'wen almost completely restored When the doors were opened at ten o'clock there were about 160 depositors waiting, and by eleven o'clock the number had not perceptibly increased. div.head: TENANTING UNFURNISHED HOUSES.
div.p: TENANTING UNFURNISHED HOUSES.

The Conservatives objected to the names of Charles Shortend, Edward Higgins, and John Henry Jakeman, who claimed the occupAtion franchis- in re6pect to their residences in Byron-street. Th., obj-etinn was short tenancy.—Mr. Fla n d ley said tile case was a rather peculiar one, the property was not finished when the three tenants took possession early in July. The lobby had not been floored or the windows completed. The landlord allowed Shortend to live in the house rent fre:., until the 27th July, and the other claitnants until the first Monday in August.—Mr. Hughes : But have they paid the.rates for the full period P—Mr. Handley : They have paid all the rates demanded of them.—Shortend corroborated Mr. Handley's statement.—The Barrister held that as the claimant had paid all the rates demanded ot him he was entitled to a vote. Be therefore allowed the claim.—At a later period Higgins appeared and Mr. Hughes elicited the fact that he had not slept in his house until the 17th July, and his name was promptly struck out. As Jakeman did not appear to sustain his claim, his name was also struck out.

div.head: AN EX-DETECTIVE EMPLOYED.
div.p: AN EX-DETECTIVE EMPLOYED.

The Conservatives made objections to a number of lodger claims in Runcorn North, the objections being supported by an ex-member of Runcorn Police force, named Woodrow. Reference was constantly made to Woodrow's book to prove the object' be and Difr. Hand- ley remarked that before he would im driven to the employment of a detective for obtaining information as to the lodger claims and the making of objections, he would be without votes for ever. He considered it a very mean way of doing business.—Wcodrow protested against such remarks; although he had been a detective he was not a detective now. AN IMPORTANT DECISIOK.

Messrs. T. D. TIMIT;in-;,-6:-A77fitTinaids, Arthur Tim- mins, arid Frank W. Timmins, claimed votes as occu- piers of the Bridgewater Foundry.—Mr Handley said the case involved two points, and the first one to be disposed of was that the business was carried on by the executors of the late Ebenezer Timmins, and only one of the.claimants was an executor. The real object of the claims was to obtain a County Council qualificathn, P 3 the whale of them were on the register for Parliament- I cry purposes.--Mr. Hughes said if the whole of the claimants were not executors, yet they were all beneficially interested, land he thought they were entitled to all the franchises for which they were qualified, notwithstanding that their names neither appeared on the rate books nor as partners in the ordinary Bet!Sl of the term.—A discussion ensued, and eventually the Barrister gave his opinion that there was nothing to debar the claimant from being registered. The second point was then brought forward, as to whether, being already on the ownership register of Runcorn North, and also for their qualification as resi- dents, they should appear on division, one or division three. —The, Barrister considered it would be safest and least likelihood of the votes being lost, if the names were allowed to remain on division one, and this was accordingly done.

div.head: COUNTY PRINTERS AND STARRINO.
div.p: COUNTY PRINTERS AND STARRINO.

In the course of the sitting Mr. Freeman, from Messrs. Philips and Golders, printers of the County Register, attendedond,referring to staternisat a rnadoat the opening of the Court at Northwich, said the fault of the stars being in the wrong place did not lie with them. They were simply put in the positions which thy occupied in the copy of the Clerk of the Pe-ce. That being so the remarks made by Mr. Handley ought to be withdrawn. --The Barrister said neither Mr. Handley, Mr. Hughes, nor himself cast any reflection upon the county printers. The accident had happened,hut he thought as there were only 15 cases out of so many hundreds, and this was the first election that had taken place since starring had come into the county registers, that there was no very great cause of complaint. Some conversation took place between the agents anti the representative of Messrs. Philips and Golder, who expressed himself satis- fied with the explanation given by the lisrrister. The proceedings were brought to a conclusion by the usual vote of thanks to the Revising Barrister for his kindness and courtesy.

div.head: RUNCORN SCTIOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCTIOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Rail, on Tuesday. Al r. .T. Pritchard presided, and there were present, the Rev. Dr. Gastaidi. Dr. McDougall, Mr. T. Handley, and Rey. Canon Wood (vicu-dhair- man), with Mr. C. Moss (clerk.) SCHOOL ATTENDANCX. The School Attendance Committee reported that 47 parents were summoned before them for infrinsement of the Education Act, and 41 appeared.—Dr. Gastaldi sug- gested that a special meeting of the Committee should be held as soon as possible in order to see whether they could not do something to secure A better attendance of children at school. He could count children in the streets by hundreds during school time.

div.head: SCIIOOE. lIANAMMIKNT.
div.p: SCIIOOE. lIANAMMIKNT.

The School ILlanagement Committee recommended that the salary of Miss Annie Acton, assistant mistress, at Greenway-rod Schools, be advanced to £5O per annum. That the resignation of Mr. J. T. Looney, certificated assistant master at Greenway-road Schools, be accepted. That the Evening School be resumed forthe winter months, on the 27th inst., and that the following teachers be appointed : Mr. J. F. Moulton,head teacher ; Mr. LV. Epps, assistant teacher ; and Mr. E. W. Rosser, assistant teacher.—The Clerk presented a financial state. merit, with respect to the net expenditure of Greenway- road Schools, during the past year, showing that the net balance from the rates was £123, of which £45 was chargeable to the abolition of school fees.—The minutes were adopted on the motion of Dr. McDougall.

MR. (I RIC& Mr. El. J. Grice wrote stating that " having ceased to be a member of the Board of the Run Born Improvement Commissioners, I resign the membership of the Science and Art Committee." He wished to express his appre- ciation of the Clerk's services and persemal effort to promote and further the interest of the Technical Edu- cation Scheme.—After some discussion as to the legal position of the Committee in regard to Mr. Grice's resign- ation, Dr. McDougall moved that the resignation be accepted with regret. Mr. Once had been a very cordial co-worker on the Science and Art Committee, and it was a matter of regret that be had ceased to be a representative. He was sure that if an opening occurred by which Mr. Once's services could be secured to the public their successors would only be too glad to have the assistance of Mr. Once, who took a deep interest in all branches of education.—Dr. Gastaldi seconded the motion. The Committee were losing a gentleman who had proved himself mofit capable in dealing with the business to be transacted by the Committee. The motion was canied.—lt was also resolved to accept as members of the Committee Messrs. F. Wiswall, .1. W. Lightburn, and E. Wynne Humphreys, who are nominated by the Board of Commissionerk

div.head: LOSS OF A. CAAINARVON SCHOONER.
div.p: LOSS OF A. CAAINARVON SCHOONER.
The schooner Erlhald, of Carnarnon, loaded with Elates, sprang a leak early on Thursday morning, twelve miles off Dungeness nct sank. The crew of twelve nen were saved, and landed at Folkestone.

div.head: MURDER AND SUICIDE BY A BOY.
div.p: MURDER AND SUICIDE BY A BOY.

VIENNA, THITItSDAY,—A most extraordinary tragedy is reported from Tarnopol, in Galacia. As the boys attend- ing a gymnasium there were leaving their classrooms at noon on Thursday, one of the youths named Johann Schwed fired a revolver with fatal effect at Dr. Felix Glowacki, one of the professors, against whom 1),- had a grudge. Having committed the deed Schwed killed I himself with a second shot.
SCIENCE AND AltT CLASSES AT
AIINCO RN.

The Runcorn School Board have again decided to establish classes at their school in Greenway-road, in connection with the Science and Art Department, and the session will commence on Monday the 26th inst. In our advertising columns will be found a complete pro- gramme of the subjects to 4,e taught, together with the names of the teachers,and the hour at which the several classes meet. The fees are very low, and opportunity is afforded the youth of the town of increasing their store of knowledge, and of improving their chances of a successful career in life. We trust the classes wil be highly successful. •
EXTRAORDINARY RECOVERY OF A STOLEN CHILD Ar RUNCORN.

The police :at Run Corn have this week investi- gated an extraordinary case of robbing of a child. For several weeks a young woman bad been seen in the town with a boy between Iwo and three years of age, but since the Bth ipnsr.unt,slie had been noticed going about without it. This coming. to the ears of the authorities, they feared that something serious might hare occured, and Sept. At herten had her brought to the Poliee Station, and cpiestioned her. She stated that the child was with Ars. Fos- ter, in one of the buts. on Frodshain. Marsh, who was taking care of it for her, and that the hally had been given to her in n lodging-house, at Bedford, six months ago, by an Irisnman who was unknown to her, and who came there with three children, the ; youngest of whom lie gave her to take care of: Sus- picious as to the truthfulness of the statements, Supt. Atherton had her detained. Her name is Elizabeth Ann Chapman, and she gives her age 17, and states that her parents resideat Stanley Point, Ellesmere Port. The chiLd was found safe and healthy on Frodsham Marsh, as stated by the young woman. It was Under the care of Mrs. Chadwick, daughter of Mr. Dennis, the missionary, on Frodsham Marsh. A child had been stolen from Rom ford, Essex, and Supt. Atherton communicated with, the police there.

On Thursday, a communication came to hand from Romford. It stated teat a boy aged two years, whilst at play in High-st. in that town on May 23rd, 1892, was stolen. His name was Albert Twitchett. The description followed, which is identical with that of the little one. Particulars of the woman who was supposed to have taken it sway, were also given and these agree with the appearance of the prisoner. The letter further states that a warrant has been issued for her arrest, and that the pluents at present are hop picking in Chemin • now acknowledges taking the child from Romford. She has been twice remanded by Mr. J. Handley and she will again be brought before the magistrates this morning.

div.head: ADJOURNED BREWSTER SESSIONS. AN APPEAL TO WARRINGTON MAGISTRATES.
div.p: ADJOURNED BREWSTER SESSIONS. AN APPEAL TO WARRINGTON MAGISTRATES.
BY TICE EDITOR. " Go, put your creed into your deed. Nor speak with double tongue."
—Emerson.

Justices' justice—say, what shall it be? You men who sit on high, and hourly note How the Drink-fiend works evil in the town, How drink and crime go ever hand in hand; You, the custodians of morality, Who lecture brazen vice, say will ye play The hypocrite, and mock at righteousnrss, By further licensing the hideous thing? What of your fellow-men, and what of mothers Who strive to make their children pure and good, Whose homes are dear to them as yours to you— Shall they be counted naught, end thrust aside While these new dens are opened in their midst? Ali, tell us, will you have them at your doors, So that your dainty daughters may touch pitch And be defiled ; so that your thriving sons , May, thoughtless, walk therein and thrive no more, But reel along life's road reckless and wrecked? What, the thought stings you ? Why then let it sting, And let it burn, until, resolved, you say— That you will do as you would be done by. Let no false bribe allure Vs hat offer they? Nothing their own—that you yourselves have lent. What! Bribe a man with his own purse? The devil ' Himself must grin at such sardonic jest., But what will burning greed of gold not do? Plant pitfalls everywhere—for gold, for gold.; Men stagger and sink, and wives and mothers fall, And tender children die the death of dogs. Asylum, workhouse, prison—how they gape ! They gape and they are filled ; the victims bleed, Suffer, and groan, and perish in their prime ; And still the Brewer's cry is gold, more gold ! And will ye, sober men of justice, hearken To the mean voice that breathes an empty bribe? Or will ye not, like Him of old, thus say— Tempter away! Get thee behind me, Satan r Warrington, September 15th, 1892.

div.head: MESSRS. W. P. AND W. SKELTON, LIMITED, WARRINGTON.
div.p: MESSRS. W. P. AND W. SKELTON, LIMITED, WARRINGTON.

The 'prospectus of this new company will he found in nur advertising columns. The capital of the company is £25,000, divided into 800 six per cent. perference shares of £lO each (cumulative and with priority in respect of capital as well as dividend), mtking £6,000, and 1,700 ordinary shares of £lO each provide for the remainder of the capital. Toe preference and ordinary shares may be paid up in full on allotment, and interest will be allowed from the date of actual payment in respect of such por- tion as may be for the time being in advance of the date of payment. The directors, it may he interesting to state, will be Messrs. W. P. Skelton, William Fairhurst, Henry Roberts, and W. J. Forshaw ; the solicitors, Messrs. Percy Davies and Forshaw ; the secretary, Mr. James Earle ; -and the bankers, Parr's Banking Company and the Alliance Bank Limited. The subscription list opens on Wednesday, and will close on or before Mon- day, the aitit September. The company has been formed to acquire and work the business carried on in Warrington and elsewhere by the successful firm bearing the name of Messrs. W. P. and W. Skelton, general iron mongers and wholesale merchants, and dealers in hardware, cycles, smallwarcs, toys, brushes, fancy goods, and foreign importing and expo, ting, of general goods. The company will acquire all the freehold land and buildings known as " The Jubilee Buildings,Horsemarket-street," valued at £5.100; the stock-in-trade, machinery, &c., valued at £10,415, as well as the book and other debts amounting to £5,600. The company will also take over the tenancy of the warehouse, tenement, building and premises occupied by the present firm at Whitechapel, Liverpool. The capital necessary for the acquisi- tion and working of the business, the freehold land, shop, goodwill, machinery, stock, itc., is estimated at 25,000. Evidence of the vitality of the concerns is afforded by the report of Mr. Arthur Bennett, chartered accountant, who has examined the books of the concern for the last four years and a half. This certificate which must be very gratifying to intending shareholders, shows that the average aggregate net profits, after making due allowance for depreciation, amounted to £3,127 us. ld. per annum. Mr. W. P. Skelton, who is retaining the whole of his interest in the business in ordinary shares, will act as managing director far ten years, and he and his brother have entered into an agreement not to enter into competition with the new company.

div.head: EXPLOSION IN A SAFE.'
div.p: EXPLOSION IN A SAFE.'

• On Thursday mnrning a gas explosion occurred in the booksafe at the offices of Messrs. Brown, Fleming and Murray, accountants, Glasgow, seriously insuring two clerks, blowing out the windows, and doing other damage. The clerks were removed to the Infirmary.

div.head: YACHTING PARTY DROWNED.
div.p: A YACHTING PARTY DROWNED.

On Thursda an inquest was held at Purilet on the bodies of Elizabeth Farris, wife of the landlord of the White Hort, Greenhithe, and Eliza Smith, Sister of Mrs. Farris, who was drowned in the river Thannes, off Pur- fleet, togethor with Harriet, daughter ot Mrs. Farris, whose body has not yet been recovered. It appears that the three deceased, with a gentleman, went for a sail in the yacht Myrtle. In putting off to the yacht the boat capsized and all the occupants were thrown into the water, the three females being drowned. A veblict of .• Accidental death " was returned.

Mr. Chamberlain and Sir John Lubbock spoke at a meeting in the Birmingham Town Hall on Wednesday evening in support of the early closing movement. Mr. Tom Maun has sent to the annual congress of the Dockers' lin* at Swansea his resignation as president of the union, and has accompanied it with an intimation that he will not, on this occasion, withdraw it, as he did last year. The announcement was received by the con- gress with expressions of profound regret.
ITHINGS HEA.RD AND SEEN
AT WARRINGTON.

Tile question of appointing additional magistrates for Warrington is, I believe, under consideration by the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster. It was rumoured that the appointments would be in time for the Licensing S4ssion next. Tuesday, but, as the day draws nigh, this bccomea very doubtful.

The Warrington Trades and Labour Council in passing a motion recently in favour of the appoint- ment of working-men magistrates have been decidedly to the front. They have in this matter taken the lead even of the Trades Congress in Glas- gow, for i observe that at that assembly a resolution has since been adopted in support of the same 1, principle. It is an excellent principle, though I fear the carrying o' it out is impracticable, just as the election of workingmen M.P.'B, to any appreci- able extent, is impracticable in the absence of p‘vmeut of members.

The Liverpool licensing authorities have deter- midedly ant their faces against the provision ot back entrances to public-houses where they do not already exist. It is to be hoped that this example will have some weight with the Warrington magis- trates, in preventing a recurrence of the contrary practice of which we have recently had such a flagrant instance on their part. To talk about being resolved nit to increase the number of licenskt public-houses while at the same time they practic- ally create a new one by allowing an hotel to have a back entrance provided for it in a thickly populated quarter, is a piece of moral c.suistry which lean- not unders.and.

It is now a number of months since " Manlius" directed attention in the "Examiner "to the high- handed breachcs of the law committed by Warring- ton magistrates in haring boys birched, when their parents on being charged with not tending them I regularly to school. plraded that it was the fault of the lads themselves. There was one element in the matter to which the writer did not draw attention, land that was that it was hardly right for magis- trates to accept the parents' testimony not given oa oath, against their children, since the former would only too frequently be ready to screen them- selves at the latter's expense, and, by letting them have a birching. save themselves cost.

I have been struck by the fact that since the denunciation of the magistrates for their procedure and the backing it got from the "School Board Chronicle." I have not sees a record of a single case of a lad being sentenced to be birched at Warring- ton.- Threats of the castigation have been innumer- able; the birch has always been hanging over truant youngsters in the court like Damocles' sword suspended by a hair, but it ha q never des- cended; ard the birch rod which once used to be IVaced in front of the Chief Constable like the , mace in front of the Speaker's chair is no more to be seen there.

It will be satisfactory toy readers to learn that there has at last been 4 declaration from the War- rington Bench and the Magistrates' Clerk—though it has come very tardily—that the Bench were wrong in the matter. On Tuesday, it seems Mr. R. Garnett was presiding at the Court, hearing cases against parents for non-compliance with the Education Acts, and was beginning to talk about a birching for the boy concerned, when Major Nicholson, who was seated on the Bench, objected to this as illegal, though wishing the law gave magistrates the power to have lads birched. The Deputy Magistrates' Clerk thereupon promptly informed the Bench that they had no power to have the youth so chastised, as there was no charge against him. So ended the matter, and I presume that now we have heard the last of magistrates and parents, after somewhat ancient fashion, making whipping boys of at least legally innocent lads, for the legal and very often the moral offences of the parents tLieraslel reg. But how came the practice to becontinued so long with the cognizance of a 3 Magistrates' Clerk?

It is unsatisfactory, however, to learn that Mr. Riley, the school attendance officer, declared that Warrington was the worst place in Lancashire for truants they being all over the town. Another argument in favour of establishing a School Board.

The "Pall Mall Gazette" had, one day this week, some very useful comments on the question of san- itation—a burning question just now. It remarks that Parliament has done about all that it can use- fully do for the present. If the truth be told, it adds, the law on the subject is a good deal in ad- vance of local public opinion. If the measures which the Statute declares it to be the duty of the local authorities to enforce were only carried out we should g 3 ahead very tepidly in the housing of the poor.

Then we are told—and I wonder if it can have any possible bearing upon Warrington—" that the passive resistance of the speculative builder and of the gentlemen who finance the speculative builder is a factor with which almost every Town Council has to reckon. We should like to see it a rule that no man interested in the local building trade should be a member of the Works Committee of any C)r- poration."

The lodger is faring rather badly at the Revision Courts this year. There s"em a diTalution to insistupon his landlord or landlady paying quite a respectable rent before admitting him upon the register. If there is anybody now-a-days who is still unconvinced of the necessity of a reform in registration law, I should- advise him just to drop into a revision court when a disputed lodger's claim is being gravely debated. The ingenious quibbling, or nibbling, of the advocates on either side, to prove the poor victim's fitness, or unfitness for the vote, and the subtle hairsplitting of the revising barrister, to justify his decision, one way or the other, is really a little too comical. 1 feel certain that visitors will come away convinced of the need of registration reform.

So far as the Liberals are concerned; it is very satisfactory to know that the revision has turned out exceedingly well for them. Mr. Clayton, the Liberal agent, is always careful in preparing his brief; and Mr. Browne, as solicitor, is equally care- ful not to let a chance slip from the moment it is placed in his hands. Then again, the ratepayers themselves, taught by the last election, have found that they lose their votes, if they do not respond to the call to attend the Court at the right time. There has been an admirable response this year, and there is therefore an admirable result.

-- . Mr. G. J. Brown, of A•pley-st., nails attention to the fact that the phonographic jubilee of Mr. T. A. Reed, the well-known shorthand writer and rey.)orter is to be celebrated this year. It is, it appears, just fifty years since, as a youth, Mr. limed began the study and practice of the art with which his name has for many years been identified. The occasion is deemed a fitting one to present Mr. Reed with some substantial testimonial, end Mr. Brown inti- mates that he will have pleasure in acknowledging any subscription that may be forwarded to ii towards the testimonial.

I notice that a National Scholarship has been obtained by Mr. Vm. Longshaw, a student of the Stockport Technical School, on the results of the examination of the Science and Art Department. Mr. hongsbaw was born and reared in Warrington. Amongst the many competitors throughout the country for the scholarships in chemistry and phy- sics Mr. Longshaw heads the list of successful candidates, and therefore, all the greater credit is due to him. The scholarship entitles Mr. Longshaw to free admission to the lectures and laboratories of the Royal College of Science at London or Dublin, for a period of three years, with a liberal allowance formaintenance during the course of study pursued there.

div.head: MERLIN.
div.p: MERLIN.
COERCION ABOLISHED IN IRELA.ND.
MR. MORLEY REVOKES MR_, BALFOUR'S PRO-

div.head: -CLAMATIONs.
div.p: -CLAMATIONs.

A special meeting of the Privy Council was held at Dublin Castle, on NVednesday, at which there were pre- sent the Chief Secretary (Mr. John Morley, M P.), the Lord Chancellor, Mr. Justice Johnson, and the Attorney- General. It was decided te withdraw all the proclama- tions issued under the Coercion Act of 1887. Nothing could more strikingly illustrate the altered rule in Ire- lend than this decision, and scarcely anything could be devised which would be so much calculated to inspire the people with confidence in the good faith of 'the Liberal loaders.

EXPECTED RELEASE OF PRISONERS. It is expected that the revoking of the Crimes Act proclamations throughout Ireland by Mr. Morley will be speedily followed by the release of all the pris ners who were convicted under the change of venue clause* of the Act.

I am lonely and sad when I'm left by myself. Though wih friends I ean never be gay; But you are quite lively and joyous and free, Please tell me the reason, I pray.

I can't get a partner to share my sad life— The ladies all answer me" I'm always depressed when they're at their best. div.head: BEFORE THE ALIGISTRA.TE3.
div.p: BEFORE THE ALIGISTRA.TE3.
THROWING PAVING SRITS INTO TIM RIVIR.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday, William Duckworth, 12, son of Thomas, 25, Mill-lane mad Benjamin Huxley, 9, son of Benjamin, Hood-lane, Sankey-st., were charged with throwing paving setts, ,belonging to the Corporation' S into the river, on unday, night.—The case having be en proved by a constable, Alderman Francomb remarked that these setts were most costly, and an enormous amount of damage might be done by throwing them into the water.—They were were Ailed 2s. 6d. each, and c•utioned.

div.head: THR CATAPULT NUISANCE.
div.p: THR CATAPULT NUISANCE.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, Thomas Cook, a boy,aged 18,was charged with discharg- ing, on Sunday, missels from a catapult in Winwick-rd., to the danger of passengers. The Chairman commented on the discharging such instruments in the public streets, and the lad was fined 58., and had to forfeit the caterp u It.
DISCHARGING FIREWORKS.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, James Bamford, aged 16, son of William, 12, Norman. et., was brought up on a charge of discharging fireworks in Chorley-st., on Saturday night. His mother, who was present, said in reply to the Bench that the lad was not at work, and his father did not want him to work at the forge. —The Chairman expressed Ns surprise at a boy of this lad's age being brought up in idleness, and remarked that it was the very way to train him up to bad courses.—The Bench adjourned the case for four weeks, the Chairman expressing the hope that in the meantime he would go to work, and observing that if they heard a better account of him they might deal favourably with him.

div.head: CHARGB OF STABBING.
div.p: CHARGB OF STABBING.

On Monday rnorning,at the Warrington borough police court, Alfred Alcock, aged 21, brewery labourer, 17, Winwick-street, Was charged before Aldermen Francomb (chairman), and Wright, with stabbing, on Saturday night, Edward Alcock, his brother, a tanner. The Ch ief- Constable said the prisoner was residing with his mother and at from a quarter to half-past 11 on Saturday night, the compkiinant was in the house. A grievance had arisen which had caused the complainant to cease to live there, about a week ago, but Dr. Brooks was attending the complainant's brother George, and as the prisoner and his mother were drunk, the doctor wished the-com- plainant to remain with his sick brother. When the &etcr had turned his back, the mother became angry, and ordered the complainant out of the house. Be said "No, I am going to stop with my brother ; the docter says I must." She laid hold of the complainant to put him out, and ultimately the defendant assisted. The complainant resisted. Blows were exchanged between him and the prisoner. A crowd got round the door, and P.C.'s Barlow and Bar- nett came, and heard Edward Adcock say he was stabbed da two places, and saw the blood running profusely from him. The prisoner was taken into custody, and the complainant was taken to the Infirmary, where he still remained, and. was unable to be in Court, though the doctor said he would be able to attend in the course of a week.—Mr. Hunt applied fora remand accordingly for a week—P.C. Bari dve deposed to the complainant telling him he had been twice stabbed, and to witness and P.C. Barnett taking him to the Infirmary, and bringing to the station the prisr4ner, who denied having stabbed the complainant, saying lam guiltless of the act. I never did it."—Tlie prisoner was remanded bra week.

div.head: SMOKE NUISANCE.
div.p: A SMOKE NUISANCE.

At the borough —msgi-strates' court yesterday, Messrs. W. A. Bishop and Co., manufactunrs of borox, Dial- street, were summoned on a charge of causing a nuis- ance by emitting black smoke from their chimney stack. Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, town clerk, appeared on behalf of the Corporrtion, and said Mr. Fleming, the manager had seen him that morning and consented to an abatement of the nuisance. A formal order was made against the defendant for abatement of the nuisance, and payment of costs. A SOLDIER CLAIMED AS AN APPRENTICE. Mr. Garner, from the office of Messrs. J. and 0. Swift, solicitors, St. Helens, Applied for an order against Col. Tarentyman for restoration to Messrs. Pilkington Bros., of St. Helena, of an apprentice who had enlisted at Orford Barracks. The defendant did not appear, and the order was made against him.

ASSAPLT ON TRH MARKET INSPECTOR. Henry Turner, 130 County-road, Walton, Liverpool, was charged with assaulting, on Wednesday, Etjali Place, Market Inspector. The defendant did not appear, Mr. J Lyon Whittle, Town Clerk, appeared for the pro- secution. He stated that the defendant, who was an auctioneer, took possession of a stall in the market, without the permission of Mr. Place, and in his absence at dinner. On his return he took possession of the goods till the defendant came back, and on his doing so demanded toll from him, as he had a right to do. The defendant abused him very much and said he had stolen the goods, and Mr. Place came to the door and was go- ing for a constable, when the defendant struck him, knocking him on his hands and knees.—Mr. Place gave evidence confirming this statement. The Town Clerk said the defendant came to hi a office on Thursday and apoligised for the assault; and if he had appeared in court and apolngissd he would not have pressed the case but as he had defied the court he pressed the proceed- ings.—Mr. Place said that defendant had apologised to him, hut he told him the case must be settled in court.— The defendant was fined £1 and costs, 41. 14s. in all.

div.head: THgFT OF A DUCK.
div.p: THgFT OF A DUCK.

Wm. Parker, Stamford-st., was brought upon remand charged with being found in possession of a dead duck, supposed to have been stolen. P.C. Cooper, 20, said he saw the prisoner with another man in Orford Avenue, on Monday, and the. prisoner had the duck in his pos- session, and handed it to the other man, who ran away and disappeared amongst s9me trees near Orford Flail. The duck had been newly killed, and he found that the prisoner on his apprehending him had blood on his Coat. The owner of the duck could not be discovered. A farmer at Orf'ord had had three stolen, but he would do nothing in [lib matter. The prisoner was bound over to come up for judgment if necessary, the duck being detained.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Mr. Voisey (in the chair) and Mr. John Gedcks. ASSAULT ON TUE POLICK—Winif red Jenninv, fustian cutter, was charged with having been drunk and dis- orderly on Friday night, and also with assaulting P. C. Cooper.—P.C. Cooper stated that on Friday night the defendant was making a disturbance near Mahe Central Station. He (Witness) went up to the defenant, when she kicked him and bit him.—P.C. Bell corroborated, and the defendant, who had been up several timers be- Lore, was sent to prison for 14 days. ' Tun' moat MRSEIRS. RYLAND!! Dims.' Samner Brooks, a labourer, at Messrs. ltylancis Bros., was charged with stealing from the works op.Siitiirday morning 'a quantity of wire netting valued at I.3;—Pri- -wrier pleaded guilty..,-The Chief Consta.ble stated . that on Saturday morning the prisoner was ctin Church-st. by P.C. Hollingsworth, who noticed that -he had some- thing bulky under his coat, and found that it was a quantity of wire netting concealed between some pieces of wood. When charged with the theft at the Police

Station prisoner made no reply.—P.C. Hollingsworth gave corroborative evidence.—Mr. J. J. Neild, manager at Messrs. Rylands's works, said that he had no fault to find with the prisoner's previous character.—A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed. THEFT OF A Puass.—Ellen Parker, a girl about 18 years of age, was charged with having stolen from the person of Harriet Hill, in Buttertnarket-st.. a purse con- taining:3s. 9d.„ on Friday night.—The prisoner, pleaded not guilty.—The Chief Constable stated that on Friday night a constable was engaged taking someone to the Police Station from Buttermarket-et., and a large crowd had gathered. The prisoner was in the crowd. and was observed to put her hand in the pocket of Mrs. Hill's dress, and then go away. The prisoner was caught near to the Police Station, where she dropped the purse on the floor and denied having stolen it, In answer to the charge, she said" I did not take it." ,The prisoner first said She come from Manchester, and then from Southport. She gave the name of Ellen Parker, and it was subsequently found that her name was Mary Burke. She had corns into Warrington from Manchester on Friday morning.—Harriet Hill said that she was in But- termarket-st. on Friday night when a person asked her if she had not had something stolen from her. She put her hand into her pocket, and found that her purse was gone. She identified the purse produced as her pro- perty.—Bridget Jeffries stated that she was coming down Scotland-road on Friday night when she felt a hand in her pocket, and turning round saw the prisoner who immediately went away. Later on she again saw the prisoner, apparently walking in company with Mrs. Hill, and then observed her suddenly go away. She (witness) went up and asked Mrs. Hill if she knew the prisoner. Mrs. Hill replied that she did not. She Ghen told her to look if she had not had something stolen from her. Mrs. Hill found that her purse was gone. They then went after the prisoner. Maggie Caslin cor- roborated the last witness's statement. —Mary Braine taid that she saw the prisoner take the purse out of Mrs. Hill's pocket. She followed her and caught her neir the Police Station.—The prisoner was sent to gaol for 14. days. MONDAT.—Before Aldermem Francomb (chairman), and

DRUNIC.—Iohn Johnson, bricklayer, 79 Buttermarket- street, drunk in Buckley-st., on Saturday night. The defendant said he took lodgings in Buckley-st., and the husband of the woman he took them from came in and put him and his tools out saying he did not keep lodgers. —That caused him to be excited.—He was fined 53. Daniel Lackey, drunk behind Cairo-st., on Saturday night. A constable said the man had got into Mr. Macaulay's back yard, though be was satisfied he had no felonious intention ; but a second man was trying to get in which he did rot like.—The defendant had to pay the lock up fee, 2s. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—BodeIia Knockton. aged 21, 53rd appearance, drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket- st., on Saturday night. She had come out of prisan on Saturday afternoon.—She said she had hal nothing to eat and the drink she had took effect on her.—The Chief Constable said prisoners were very weak as a rule when they left prison; and they were drunk in no time if they took drink.—Alderman Francomb said it was horrid that one so young should have spent five years and nine months in jail as the prisoner had.—She was discharged on premising to behave better.—William Connor, drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-st., on Saturday night, was fined 5. and costs.—John Garvey, in the same street, that night, ss. and costs. —John Macmahon and George Kent. in Buttermarket-st.. on Sunday night,were , fined ss. and costs.—Patrick Moore, on Pinner's Brow on Sunday night, was fined 103. and costs. A con- stable said they were running about and shouting. and asking for checks from people vrho came out Of the Theatre. They made a noise with their months at wit- ness, and shouted "Slop."—They were fined 23. 6d. each, and cautioned. ALLOWING HORSES TO STRAY.—Thomas Lawless Was charged with allowing three horses to stray in Museum- street on Sunday morning.—Sergeant Taylor found them there about 4 a.m. He was fined 2s. liid. for each horse.

ArrEsyartov.—Frederick Cousins, aged 19, was charged with fraudulent enlistment, by false attes- tation, in the Liverpool regiment of militia. He was sent to jail for 11 days. Darnis AND DISORDERLT.—Theresa Oultram, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Orford-lane on Monday night.—A Constable said she was shouting and using most filthy language towards her husband.— Her husband corroborated, and asked for a separation, saying his life was unendurable with her. His wife charged him with ill-usage of her.— The Chief. Constable said the man was very well known as-a sober industrious man, and his wife was very much given to drink.— She was censured before a tribunal only a few weeks ago, for overlying a child under very ugly circumstances.—She was sent to jail for 14 days with hard labour.—The husband again begged for a separation but the magistrates' told him they could not grant that.—Annie Ryan, Kate Flannery, late of St. Halons, Catherine Carney, Peter Higgins, were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Smith-street, early that morning. The evidence disclosed that they were singing and shouting in the street in a most disgraceful , manner, and had brought all the neighbours out into the street.—They were sent to prison for seven days' hard labour each.

div.p: some fine passing between Faulkner Crompton, and Pendlebury, again ran the ball in the Yorks quarters. Duckett and Bring,: got the ball away, but P. Riley showed up finely with a good dribble. The Bradford, backs got hold, and some really fine passing between Bailey, Popplewell,and Richard gave the latter a chance, of which he availed himself by searing at the corner flag. Firth took the place, but no goal resulted. Faulkner restarted, and Pendlebiary was soon off with a strong/run along touch, Fieldhoune pulling hint up. Still the game was very exciting, bath teams playing grandly. Briggs, Popplewell, and Duckett initiated another raid on the Cheshire fines, and Richard again. scored, but if Firth again failed, no sooner had Faulkner kicked off than Bradford again attacked. Half-time score :—Bradford 2 tries, Runcorn 1 try. Upon resuming, Hampson missed the lira, but Faulkner got up. Duckett was nearly in, but Hotighten was safe, and the Runcorn forwards came away.grandly, and Robinson held Poppiewell before he cola get in a return, and a huge punt of Houghton forced a minor point. Popplewell got hold and evaded all .ppositibri until Houghton grassed him. G. Robinson relieved the prensure a little, but Bradford were not to be denied, another minor being forced. Toothill next essayed to break through, but was safely held, Faulkner tackling brilliantly. Runcorn now got a free kick, and Crompton tried to goal, but Fieldhouse ran the ball out. Runcorn pressed,but could not score,and thename ended Bradford 2 triesfßioncorn 1 try. WIDNES Sr. MADE'S V. RDNCORIV A.—This 4 match was played at Widnes before a, small attendance. The bonsesters kicked off, but Webb obtained possession and ' after a fine run, passed to Antrobus who scored" behind the posts. Runcorn continued to force the game, but the home defence was good, and play was gradually taken to the other end, but nothing resulted. The game became a very tame one, and at half-time the score stood —Runcorn, 1 try ; St. Mary's nil. From the. re-start Widnes broke away, but were soon forced ontheciefen- sive, and from a fine passing movement between Limb, Autrobus, and Dunbavand, the last-named scored under the posts, and a kick at goal was charged down.. Antro- bus scored a third try two minutes later, but no goal resulted. Shortly afterwards, J. Faulkner added a, fourth try for Runcorn, and the game ended in an easy win for the visitors. Final result :—Runcorn A. 4 tries,(irpoints) Widnes nil.

WARRINGTON Sr. MARX'S v. PEMBERTON Rhearburrorr. —On Saturday, St. Mary's journeyed to Pemberton, to play the Recreation. The homedters kicked off; and the ball was at once taken to the home line, but the Rtes., with some strong forward play, took the ball to mid- field, where some good play was witnessed bettveen the backs of both teams. The visitors' forward il dribbled the ball up the field, and had hard lines in not scoring, the ball being kicked dead. The oval being again-started it was taken into the Saints' 25; where the Warrington backs showed some good passing, experiencing: hard 'lines, the ball being kicked dead as the Saints were on the point of scoring. The whistle now blew for half- time, neither side having scored. On turning rmind,the vistors started the ball, and the game became very fast, the ball travelling srom one end of the field to the other. The homesters now playing up strongly were soon press- ing, but the defence of the visitors being good the-Rtes. could not score, and the Saints soon took the ball clewn the field, where one of their backs made a good run„but was tackled by the full back, the Saints forcing another minor. Tht Recs. dropped out, and soon took the ball up the field, where Sharpe scored, the point nob being improved.. After the drop-ont the visitors tried hardtto make make matters equal, but had to retire defeatedAry one try to three minors.

LANCASHIRE ALLIANCE.—HINDLRY v. FIATDOCE.—TIie old opponents once more antagonised each other on the, Ladies-lane enclosure, at Hindley, on Saturday, befere 608 spectators. There has always been a large amount' 'of rivalry existing between these two clubs which was 'further enhanced on Saturday by the fact that the pee— VIERS week both teams had each won their Alliance match. Hindley takino• six goals to one out of Skertozr at Rindlev, and Flaydock defeating the Alliance chem. Iphone at Lytham by one goal to none. Both teams were fully represented and the fact that over 100 spectators travelled over frern Flay'dock shows that a hard and determined fight was anticipated, and as it turned 'out the spectators got their money's worth. After the Hay-- dock team had been kept waiting twenty minutes for the, arrival of some of the home eleven the coin was spun' the Hayclock captain winning, and placed the men with the sun at their backs. Payne commenced operations for the home team which were for some time carried on in Midland.althnolit the pace was very fast. Haydeck were the first to show up, Clark sending a long ground shot which went wide. A few minutes before the end, from a mis-kick by one of the Flaydock backs, Flindley 'scored their third point, winning their second Alliance ' match by three goals to one after a desperate fight.

Rurreoati Y. Navtrox-LE-WILLows.--This match was played on the ground of the former on Saturday. before a fair number of spectators. The visitors, who brought a strong team. started the game. The home players, who have formed a new organization. have bad few oppor. tangles for practice. At the start the visitors showed gond combination, and completely nonplussed the home side, thereby tepidly putting on three goals. After this reverse the home team brightened up considerable. and at the change of ends the score read Newton-le-Willows 3, Runcorn 1. After the interval the homesters strove. desperately to wipe out the inequality, but although they fairly penned their opponents in their own territory they could only score one more goal, the final score thus read- ing Nete(M-le-Willows. 3 :Runcorn, 2. The home team added'anotiletr, and a good game =fled in favour of Litherland he seven Trials to five. For ' Warrington. div.p: FOOTBALL.'

•,,* Secretaries of Football (Rubs are requested to note that reports o matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY. WARRINGTON v. ROCHDALE ST. CLEMENTS.

Following their victory over Dewsbury, the Warring- tonians journeyed from their native heath on Saturday, when they met Rochdale St. Clements. It had never been the good fortune of our local team to lower the Saints 'colours on their own ground, and of the previous matches played, the Rochdale men claimed a victory in the initial engagement, whilst last season's match resulted in a draw. Like Warrington, the Rochdale men had won their first match in handsome style, and it was with some amount of confidence that the Saints' enthusiasts predicted an absolute victory for their team. It was 410 Wore Waugh set the oval in motion. Evans first showed up with a sterling run, which changed the scene of operations, and short rushes by the Warrington forwards were followed by Fair. Turner get- ting bold from a line-out, and it looked big odds on him scoiing, when a hasty pass was mulled and the Saints , cleverly saved. L. Rigg cleared temporarily, but no sooner accomplished this than Boacow responded, and the ball was in dangerous proximity to the home goal again. Nolan and W. Rigg passed well at this point,and the visitors' quarters were reached. This was supple- mented by W. Rigg, Greea wood, and Ramsbottom in- dulging in some transfers, and only the fine tackling of Flumpton spoiled an otherwise excellent chance. Ashton led his men back to their original position of attack, and from now to the call of half-time the visitors maintained a footing in the Rochdale quarters. Bate and Evans initiated a movement which saw Beesom and Potts run- ning ton near the line, whilst from a scrimmage Evans was unfortunate in slipping when all opposition had been overcome. Every manceuvre was tried by the Warringtonians to cross- the line without avail, and eventually Ilurnpton failed to stay a short rush, and Boscow was passed, but the Warrington back quickly recovered himself, and a good kick and a quick follow- up by Donohue saw L. Rigg once more saving. A neat bit of play by Ileesom and Nevins gained at least 25 yards, and the former from, a pass tried a shot at goal, which went wide. Even play followed the drop out, and another accurate bout of passing by Evans and Bate saw the former again pulled down on the line. A penalty kick against Warrington gained nothing, and from amidst a stock of opponents Eleesom had another drop at goal, a minor only resulting. Plumpton met the drop-out with a ponderous kick. whilst Jolley, Bandies, Frank furner, and Ashton dribbled well, and exchange kicking saw L. Rig piloting in touch at half- way, half time arriving with'Warrington two minors to their credit.

On resuming the Saints early on showed signals of distress. The fast pace and constant hard work the Warringtonians had subjected them to began to tell their tale. Direct from the kick-off the visitors were on the Rochdale line, and, try as the homesters would, they could not clear. Warrington experienced hard lines in not scoring more than they really did, and Nevins was decidedly unfortunate in having a couple of points disallowed. After Bate, Potts, and Evans had put in some good work, the latter made a fine run al.-mg the popular track, and, being foiled near the line, Ashton was successful in getting in near the corner, the kick failing. A third minor resulted from another run by Potts, and then came a brilliant exhibition by the whole of the Warrington forwards, L. Itigg fielding the oval well,, and saving his lines at a critical juncture. Heesom next brought the Rochdale back down finely, and some clever work by Jolley, Holmes, !'air. Turner, and Berry saw the former get away in a rush dizectly after ; and passing to Ashton on the line, the Warrington skipper landed the second try. The Stints made an effort near the close, but Plumpton beat them back, and the game terminated—Warrington, 0424 ; Rochdale St. Clement's, nil. _ _

Teams :—Warrington : Boscow, back; Plumpton, Reesom, and Potts, three.nuarters ; John Bate and Evans, half backs; Ashton, Fair Turner, Frank Turner, Nevins, Jolley, Randles, Holmes Berry, and Donohue, forwards. Rochdale :L. Rigg,. back; W. Rigg, Green- wood, and Ramsbettom, three-quarters; Hallewell and Nolan, half backs; Waugh, Dex, Hil, Holt, Farmer, H. Rigg, R. Ashw•rth, E. Ashworth, and W. Oddie, for- wards. WARRINGTON " A "y. ROCHDALE ST. CLEMENT'S "A." —A splendid day favoured the opening fixture of the above teens. Warrington winning the toss decided to take advantage of the wind and the glowing orb of day, while Rochdale placed the oval in position, and hostili- ties commenced. For the first five minutes a series of scrimmages ensued, and then by a splendid bit of pass- ing between Rowe, Laity; and J. P. Lawless, the venue of the struggle was transferred into their opponents' half, when Lally seizing possession eluded several oppon- ents, and the ball la:.comiog loose, the younger Lawless smartly took it and ran in, Ashurst placing a goal. After resuming from centre, Rochdale effected a pretty piece of passing, Barton handing over the ball at the right moment to Simms, who quickly made tracks for the goal. With the game wandering about the home 25, Waugh tried to score by dropping a goal, but failed, and the ball finally found its way to P. Lawless, who put in a tall kick, end Westall, Hampsen, Bailey, and Buck. ley forced the attackers to defend. Then West all rushed over, but was forced into touch-in-goal. This episode was succeeded by a rush in which Glover, Thornley, Teare, and Davies were notable, and P. Law- less kicking across, Bailey rushed over and gained a capital try. Another pretty display of passing by the Rochdale backs was witnessed, Barton being very conspicuous, which Taylor used to such advantage that he raced to the full back before he was foiled, and an attack was prosecuted with much vigor ny the Saints. Twice Ashurst and .1. Lawless cleared, but Taylor with a capital swerving run renewed the pressure, though the defence was too good, and ultimately Glover, Teare, Higharn, and Molyneux relieved the impending danger. A clever dribble by the visiting forwards, assisted by Barton, again carried the warfare into the home quarters, when the Warrington goal was almost lowered from a free kick. Ashurst ran the ball out, and mainly owing to the efforts of Thornley, Glover, Hammon, and Higham' the opposite end of the ground was visited, and a minor forced. Directly afterwards Lally got splendidly away, and the culmination of his efforts, supplemented by a fine screw kick by Lawless, gave Rowe a try,and at half-time WiFrington led by 1-2-2 to nil. Following the usual rest Rochdale attacked, but P. Lawless with a fine run recovered the lost ground. A tong dribble by Rochdale was grandly frustrated by Ashurst, but play of an unimportant nature followed for some time. With the game careering about the centre, Molyneaux got possession, and after running close to the line, passed out ' finely to Rowe, who re-passed, but the ball and a grand opportunity were lost. Higham, Davies, Buckley, and Bailey were then prominent, but Hill temporarily cleared his lines. The back division of the home team again asserted itself, Rowe initiating a piece of beacit- fully-timed passing. between Lally. J. and P. Lawless, which enabled the elder brother to have a walk in. Lally was quiekly prominent by one of his inimitable ' runs, and again receiving the ball from Rowe ran in, and a capital game ended Warrington 1-4-5 to nil.

div.head: RUNCORN V. BRADFORD.
div.p: RUNCORN V. BRADFORD.

• This important match was played at Park Airenue, Bradford. The game caused a great amount of inter- est, some thousands of spectators being present. The teams were fairly representative. The weather was beautifully fine. The kick-off was advertised for 3.30, but it was almost four o'clock before a start was effected. Bradford won the toss, and Faulkner kicked off, Runcorn having to face the wind and sun. Duckett returned, to which Houghton punted to touch. Brad- ford had the best of the opening Crompton being forced to touch down. Faulkner and P. Riley tackled well, and Popplewell was forced into touch by Pendlebury close to the Cheshire lines. Dobson got a free kick in a favourable position, but only a minor accrued. sugden was prominent with some good kicking, which again endangered the Runcorn lines. Abrams got nicely away, but a pass forward spoiled the-chance, passing between Duckett and Dobson, gaining but little ground. Crompton got well away, and kicked to Fieldhouse ; Pendlehury raced and prevented a return. Crompton again ran well into the Bradford quarters. Pendlebury ran strongly and should have passed to Cromp- ton, who would certainly have scored: Run- corn were now pressing Bradford strongly, and after some splendid passing between the Cheshire backs, Crompton gave to Pendlebury on the line and the latter having no opposition, scored the first try. Houghton took the place, but failed to add. Richards and Toothill rushed away, but T. Robinson was safe, and

div.head: OLDEST MAN IN ENGLAND.
div.p: THE OLDEST MAN IN ENGLAND.

An oldsoidier named Amos Jinks, a native of Newport Shropshire, but no* living at Wellingborough, .North- amptonshire, is alleged to be 107 years old. The claim to such an extraordinary age has been tested, it is said, and ha's been verified to the satisfaction of the persons making the inquiries. The old man is withered, thin, and stooping ; his eyesight has failed, and his voice is shaky, but in other respects he is well, and so free from physical infirmity that he promises to go on living vat for some years to Come. Re can eat, drink, and steep as well as a man in iniddle life, and is not very deaf. Throughout his life he has been accustomed to rough outdoor work, for some years as a soldier in the Royal Artillery and at other times as an agriculttual labourer or a bricktnaker, Jinks himself did net think the fact that he was going on living, so much beyond the ordinary limit was anything remarkable until Ave years ago a local newspaper published the fact that he was 102, and his employers then lightened his work. He has been three times married, smokes, and is a moderate drinker. A fevy years ag. he buried his dwaghtern who was nearly 80.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. FOOTBALL.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. FOOTBALL.

Only two games have as yet been played; in the Lan- cashire Cup Competition, and both have resulted in a draw. The form of the players is not, however, so highly developed as the spectators may desire, but all that will be changed in a few weeks, and when the re- cords get into a stage that may be termed exciting the fun will be furious.

It is, says the " Athletic News," currently reported that the Lancashire Referees' Society are subscribing for a couple of suits of mail armour for the use of the , referees who will be sent out to wave the judicial hand and blow the judicial whistle in some of the nsatches in the near future in connection with the Leagues

• Only once during the past bur seasons have More- cambe succeeded in defeating St. Helm; Recreation, and the " glassmakers" journeyed to that pleasant watering place on Saturday determined not to be caught napping agairf. The Morecambites were much elated at having beaten BradfArd on the previous Saturday, and,were very hopeful of success this time. rhat they bad good grounds for their confidence was shown by tha. result— an even draw of a try each.

St. Helens Recreation mean making a good record this season. They have the choice of all last season's players, and are giving a trial to two or three new men, who, if they maintain their present form, will make the team as strong as ever it was. Pyke, their International for- ward, has definitely promised to turn out again for his old club, and is expected to take the field against Mossley on Saturday. The club's old secretary—Mr. Jbhn Wood —who was in office a season or two ago, when the team made its reputatiop, has been induced to return to his old position, and altogether the club's supporters are are sanguine of success.
Clarke, the late Widnes three-quarter, was down to assist both Awnll and Pemberton on Saturdny, bat at the last moment he turned out :for the Wigan club. Will he remain there P_

The straight-laced attitude which the Rugby Union Committee are taking up regarding the expenses of players, comnaitteemen, and others is not viewed with satisfaction in some quarters. The confining of allow- ances to third-class milway fares, and the giving of powets to the Rugby Union treasurer to reduce ex- penses bills are particularly obnoxious rules. The Yorkshire Committee for one intend taking a firm stand against the power to " dock " bills being left in the hands of the Rugby Union official. Such regulations as th4t are a strange commentary on the freedom of amateur football, and gives colour to the charge that we are at the bottom really a nation of humbugs.

Sunderland went through the whole of last season without making a draw, but in their second League match the spell is broken. The champions, rather sur- prikd the football world by running up half-a-dozen goals against Accrington, but their subsequent perfor- mances were not particularly brilliant, far they only beat the Celts by a goal ; and the most they. could do with Newcastle East End was to make a draw, while on Saturday Notts were pretty nearly beatiug them.

Three of the Lancashire members of the League each came in for a reverse on Saturday, Everton, the Rovers, and Accrington all finishing on the wrong side. NobodY expected the "Reds "to win at Sheffield, nor the Revers at Wolverhampton, hut Everton should have done better at Perry Barr. It will be remembered that last season heat the Villa in both engagements, so that they have lost two points where they won two twelve months ago. There is a general feeling that Everton will want some new backs ere long.

div.head: CRICKET.
div.p: CRICKET.

It was rather curious to find those people who have been cryine aloud for the county cricket championship to be decided by statistics so utterly floored when the figures did come out. These almost to a man were in favour °Watts against Surrey, whose supporters were quite content to leave well alone.

Notts were not Aven second on the list ón this method of scoring, a position enjoyed by Laneashire, who are very little behind the leaaing eleven. 'Taken on the proportion of rune saored as against those of their op- Ponents, Surrey have made 148 to their rivets, 1 Lancashire come next with 143. Notts have 1.33, and Somerset 118.

This systPm shows the value of a team's battine• and bowling alike, as both have to be taken into considera- tion. Such, according to some people, minor matters RS wins, draws, and losses are thus entirely ignored, and a county's place in the list is entirely dependent on its eenPral all-round play. This system shows how correct have been those who insisted that Lancashire ought to have done much better.

Up to the present eight cricketers have obtained over a thousand runs in important matches this summer, the number being the largest on record since 1836. The happy men are-Shrewsbury and Gunn, of Notts ; H. T. Hewett, and L. C. H. Palairet, of Somerset : S. W. Scott, and A. E. Stoddart, of Middlesex ; W. G. Grace of Gloucestershire; and W. W. Bead, of Surrey ; whilst if Abel in his second innings at Hastings succeeds in scor- ing nine, a similar hormur will be gained by the Surrey professional. It is a remarkable coincidence that so far the distinction of making the highest aggregate is shared by H. T. Hewett and A. E. Stoddart, each of these gentlemen haying scored exactly 1,402 runs.

Once more Mr. W. G. Grace has earned the proud distinction of scoring a thousand runs in first-class matches during the/cricket season, the innings of 56 which he played at Hastings for the gentlemen against the players having brought his aggregate to 1,050. Mr. Grace, of course, has often exceeded this number, but considering that he is now in his forty- fifth year, and that his highest score this summer was 99, his achievement bears eloquent testimony to the excellent and consistent nature of his betting. The success of the greatest cricketer the world has ever known in the liter years of his career Will. ha warmly welcomed wherever the game is played.

The aeronauts experienced great difficulty in effecting a landing. Throughout; Mon- day afternoon and night a crowd armed with guns and other weapons held possession of the quay, and threat- ened to throw into the water anyone who snug* to land. Towards nightfalFa Mr. Thomson left the WSWI and, approaching the landing stage in a boat, earweatly appealed for consideration on behalf of 200 women and children suffering from hunger, exhaustion, and exl posure. He said they should return to the vessel' if Permitted to land for rest and one meal.
