div.head: FIVE DEATHS RN NEW YORK.
div.p: FIVE DEATHS RN NEW YORK.

,Isnivr Toxin, WEDNESDAY.—EIorae excitement was caused this afternoon by the announcement of the Health Board that five of the deaths which occurred in this city during the past week werettuso to genuine Asiatic cholera. It was suspected at the thne the persons died that the cause was cholera, but the Health Board denied it until bacteriological examination of the intestinal fluids taken from the bodies left no doubt. All the vic- tims lived in a thickly-settled, squalid section on the east side °retie city.
The steamer Heligoland, from tetltona, on the Elbe, arrived to-day reporting two deaths from cholera among the crew.-

No new cases have been reportal from the other ships in quamntine,.and most of these will be released soon. The Norhiannia's passengers are now comfortably lodged on Flre Island, and are promised release to- morrow or the next day. The Rugres passengers after witnessing the experiences of the rtormannia's, neg to be allowed to remain aboard until the period of de- tention expires_ BERLIN, W'EINCESDAY NlGllT.—Another case of cholera has occurred in Berlin. It is stated that a barge on which a marrlied was at Hamburg a, fortnight ago. Eight persons pre.sonting choleraic symptoms have been received at the Moithit HospitaPsince Tuesday, but in no case havAsiatic choiara been ascertained. RAVAGES AT HAMBURG.

At Hamburg 344 fresh cases of cholera and 148 deaths were officially registered on Tuesday. Of theme 198 and 96 respectivelY belong to the previous. day. The num- ber taken to the hospital was 137, and 47 bodies were conveyed to the mortuaries. Hamburg, harbour is nearly free from cholera, as only one person, .a negro stoker on an English vessel, has been seized with cholera there within the last Prin. days. In the country surrounding Hamburg 15 fresh cases and 3 deaths occurred. There were 2 deaths at Harburg, 1 fresh case at Wandsbeck, and 12 fresh cases and 5 deaths at Altona.

It is stated from Wamburg that at to-day's meeting of the House of Burgesses the Senate submitted an urgent motion ,asking fer a credit for the assistance of the suffering population. It is said that ZSIXOOO is the sum demanded. FlYe thousand persons in tAltona are said to be without employment or means of subsistence, and aid for these unfortunate people is urgently requested, especially as the relief committees hithertl formed deal solely with the distress in Hamburg. Two more cases of cholera are officially announced from' Stettin, and one tq the patients has already succumbed. One death of cholera is reported from the Wolgast,road. A curious report comes from Lubeck. The doctors who till Satur- day exercised the sanitary control at the railway sta- tions withdrew from their posts on that day, in conse- quence of a disagreement with the sanitary office. Their functioas are at present being performed by police- men.

div.head: DIMINISHING IN FRANCE.
div.p: DIMINISHING IN FRANCE.

PARIS, WEDNESDAY NIDFIT.—Thp cholera. returns go on diminishing. In Havre yesterday there were seven deaths, but only two fresh cases. The Paris returns for yesterday are 33 new cases. Of these Ig werf7 fatal, and there were also Eye deaths of older patients. There were 26 cases in the nuterring, six of which were fatal, and also 21 deaths from earlier attack. MADRID, WdON'ESDAY.—The Spanish Governmeat!as been led by the reports of its Consuls and by the out- criers of the Madrid Press to believerthat the British Government and authorities take insufrrcient precau- tions against cholera. In consequence the " Official Gazette " publibties decrees ordering!aff vessels arriving from Great Britain, Gibralter, and the British Mediter- ranean possessions, to be sent to lazarettos, where they will suffer rigomus quarantine. Alf travellers and merchandise coming from England and Gihralter will undergo medial inspection and fumigation. -

ANTwIRr, WEDNIiqD IY NIGHT. —The number of cholera patients admitted to the hospital during the past twenty-four hours has increased from 3to 4, and there have been 3 deaths compared with 1 On the previous day.

- - - Sr. PETEIRSEDRO, Snrr. 14.—1 n consequence of the decrease of cholera, the Minister of the Interior has dis- continued the despatch of doctors to the infected dis- tricts. IA some of the provinces, however, the epidemic is still very prevalent, particularly in Voronesh. Kazan. Samara, Stratoff, the Don territory and Orenburg, the number of cases daily in each of these governments averaging from 309 to 600 and tha deaths from 100 to 300. In the Caucasus about 1,550/cases and 750 deaths occur daily. In St. Petersburg yesterday there were 61 cases and 15 deaths, while 54 patients recovered. AMSTERDAM, SEPT. 14.—Fresh deaths from cholera in Holland are reported to-day. BRUSSELS, SEPIC. 14.-9 fresh death from cholera has occurred in a suburb of this city.

div.head: SUICIDE AT PRESCOT.
div.p: THE SUICIDE AT PRESCOT.

An inquest was held en Saturday at the Derby Arms Jon, Eccleston-street, Prescot, by Mr. S. Brig- house, county coroner, on the body of. Edward James, forty years of age;., upholsterer, Moss-street, Prescot. The sister-in-law, named Hutchin, identi- fied deceased, who, though addicted to drink, had been pretty steady during the past six months, and appeared a late anxious on account of his wife' health.—J. Cawley, barman of the Derby Arms, said deceased called on Thursday afternoon at half-past one and had a bottle of cider. He was sober, and, after drinking it, went out, returning in about five minutes. He called for a ginger beer, and asked to see Thomas Gore, for whom he paid far a pint of beer.—Thomas Gore, labourer, said that whilst talking together he saw deceased put something into his glass, at the same time saying, " I'll show you how to take salts." His atten- tion was called away, and he heard vomiting in the ! yard. On going there he saw it was deceased, who said he would be all right in a few minutes. He after that saw him lying in the washhouse. He knew deceased for three years in St. Helens. He was a steady man.— Mr. Beaumont, licensee of the Derby Arms, said he was called to see deceased in the washhouse. Deceased told' him he felt faint. He took him a glass of water, and sent for Drs. Green and Hall. On going back to the bar he picked up a paper labelled " Oxalic acid," together with some grains of acid.—Agnes Jones, fourteen years of age, residing with her sister at Harrison's drug stores, Eccleston-street, said deceased came to the shop at a quarter to two, and asked for two ounces of oxalic acid to clean brasses, for which he paid 21d. She told him toe careful, as it was poison. In answer to the coroner she said he did not look drank. She served in the absence of the manager, who was at dinner.—Mr. Joseph Dixon, manager for Messrs. P. and W. Harrison, St. Helens, of their branch at Prescot, said he had been qualified thirty-seven years, but could not tell if the Sale of Poisons Act specified who could or could not sell.— The Coroner advised him to get a copy of the Act, and read it at once.—The jury returned a verdict GE" suicide whilst in an unsound state of mind."

div.head: CREMATION IN MANCHESTER.
div.p: CREMATION IN MANCHESTER.

'The second cremation since the opening of the Man. 'Chester Crematorium took place the other • day. The 'remains were those of Mr. Samuel Ingham, of Brf dbury, formerly of Manchester. In the hall of the building the burial service of the Church of England was read by the Hew. H. A. Noel, Longsight. At the first cremation the ashes of the deceased, enclosed in an urn, were returned to his executor, but in this case the urn was allowed to remain in the Crematorium, where it will be placed in one of the memorial niches to be provided for that Purpose.
ALLEGED MURDER BY AN OLD MAN.

John Coffey, aged 76, is in custody at Ballyduff, near Tullatnore, charged with causing the death of his wife. It is alleged that the couple 'quarrelted because Coffey made a will leaving his effects to his brothers, and that during the quarrel he struck Mrs. Coffey a blow on the head with a stick, from the effects of which .she died. Coffey, who is a small farmer, is several years older thin his wife.

div.head: SHOCKING OUTRAGE IN IRELAND.
div.p: SHOCKING OUTRAGE IN IRELAND.

On Saturday two young men of The farmer class' named Richard and Thomas Burke, where charged, before Mr. Bruen, R.M., at Thurles, with having killed Patrick Burke, who held a big farm at Ballyboy. The evidence showed that for a long time a very bad feeling had prevailed between the two families. A few days ago the prisoners and deceased were in Thurles selling cattle, and on going home Patrick was waylaid and beaten an violently that he died two hours afterwards. Prisoners were returned to the winter assizes on the 'charge of wilful murder.
THE DOUGLAS HOTEL TRAGEDY.

George Barker James Cooper, of Manchester, who is detained in the Isle of Man gaol, he having been corn- initted to take his trial for the murder of his wife Edith Annie Cooper, of Birmingnam, by stabbing her in abed- room of the Regent Hotel, Douglas, on the 3rd inst., IR being treated with the greatest consideration. His meals are being supplied from the Falcon Cliffe Hotel, opposite the gaol, and are of choice quality. He is also allowed a *part of champagne per day and unlimited cigars, and is permitted to sleep on a spring mattress and to wear his own clothes. Of course his friends provide his meals, wine, cigars, and mattress. On the island any prisoner en commi tal for an alleged criminal offence may, ,01) to conviction or discharge, procure similar privi- leges.

GRABBING NORFOLK BROADS AGAIN.

There are landlords whir want to enclose the Norfolk Broads, as there are and have been landlords whose pre- datory instincts are directed against commons. Mr. H. Gibbon Pritchard writes :—On Saturday a party of four of us rowed dews to Ranworth Broad, which I consider the most beautiful of all the broads, and found the entrance blocked up by a chain. As we knew there was another entrance further down, we rowed round to that, Ind got on to the broad in that way. As we were com- ing off, a man, evidently a gamekeeper, rowed up to us, .atid told us that we had no business to go on the broad and disturb the wild fowl. We asked him by what 'authority the entrance to the broad had been chained UP, and he told us that Squire Farmer'had said that he Would have the chain put up and chance it. Two years ago was on this broad, and the entrance was open,and we were allowed to row about undisturbed. This chain ban only been put up two or three months, and if people do not protest against it, one of the finest broads may be entirely closed to the public. The broad is affected bY the tide, the rise and fall of the water being eight or ithms Inches."

At Leeds, on Tuesday, George Cregan (26), was rc- manded, charged with causing the death of Thomas Watson. Both men, it is said, drank heavily on Satur- day, and afterwards quarrelled and fought, with a fatal result.

div.head: SELECTED READINGS.
div.p: SELECTED READINGS.

A Cm OF THE Pram:rms.—The following account, given by Fuller, of a city labouring under the horrors of plague, cannot be perused without exciting a painful interest :—" We were," says he, In his 'Turkish Tour, "closely confined within the walls of the consulate, and all persons from without were as rigidly excluded. The gate which opened from the court into the street was strictly closed,. and the only communication was through a hatch. door cut in it. The key of this was not entrusted even to the servants. Each of the company took charge of it in his turn for a day, and it was his business to see that everything supposed capable of communicating the contagion was duly purified before it was allowed to pass into the house. These precautions were at any rate ' useful, as giving a feeling of security; but I have no doubt that the distinction between such objects as are called • susceptible' (to use the tech- nic,al phrase) and such as are not, is frequently arbitrary, and that the index expurgatorius in this, as in other instances, is tinged by prejudice and caprice. Happily, some of the articles of most frequent use, such as bread, iron, and wood, for•ex- ample, were allowed to pass without suspicion;. but meat and all animal substances, and money of every kind, were thrown with iron tongs or shovels into a large tub, and compelled to pass through the watery ordeal. Letters, books, and papers, on the other band, are purified by fire, or at least by smoke, beibg placed on 'a sort of chafing-dish, and fumigatSel•with a compound of drugs, which is anything but aromatic; and if it should be necessary to affix a signature to any document, a plate of glom is intro- duced between the paper and the band of the writer. The cats, who in their nocturnal rambles are supposed to carry with them the seeds of contagion, are condemned to indiscriminate slaughter when- ever they are seen creeping along the walls or on the house-tops; and when terror is at its height, even the flies are objects of alarm, and the spots of Domitian are revived." .

THE POET CHABBB. —The late Rev. George Crabbe died in the 88th year of his age. He was a native of Aldeburgh, where his father held a situa- tion in the customs. Bred up to the profeEsion of physic, he for some time practised as a .urgeon in his native town; but disliking his pro fe6sion, he quitted Aldeburgh, and repaired to the metropolis, where he arrived without having formed any par- ticular plan, but where he hoped, that the exertion of his talents might enable him to succee.4. Whilst in London, he obtained an introduction to the Right Hon. Edmund Burke, who, struck wit-hike talents he displayed, introduced him to some of the first characters of the age, and among otipers to the late Duke of Rutland, Lord Thurlow, Dr. Johnson, and Sir Joshua Reynolds. Owing to the arbstantial favour of the former nobleman, he was induced to take orders in 1781. In 178% after the death of his noble patron, he was presented by Lord Thurlow, on the recommendation of the Duchess Dowager, to the rectories of Min- ton, in Leicester, and of West Allington, in Lincolnshire. In 1814, on the presentation of the late Duke of Rutland, he was instituted to the valuable rectory of Trowbridge. During his first acquaintance with Mr. Berke, and under his imme- diate auspices he published his poem, "The Village." After an interval of twenty-two years, he again ap- peared before the public as the author of the "Parish Rarister." It) 181 Q, he published "The Borough ;" 'Mies hiVent ;" in 1819, "tides of* Hall ;"--works of which their highest excellence is their truth to nature, but nature 9:t her homely garb. In private life, Mr. Crabbe was modest, re- tired, and unassuming; feelingly alive to the miseries of his fellow•creatures, he devoted no small portion of his time to their alleviation; and in doing this, united to his ministerial his medical character, and tluis rendered himself beloved and useful in a two-fold capacity. Mr. Crabbe was married ,in 1783 to Miss Elmy, one of the daughters and co- heiress of the late Tovell, Esq., of Parham, by whom he left children.

SOLI:ITEM' FUNERAL'S.—There is a simplicity and a decency in a military funeral, even in its plainest form, far surp issing in solemnity all the pomp and pageantry of the most sumptuous funeral In cival life. There, a number of hirelings, whose' bodies only bear the garb of woe, while their countenances, gestures, and manner, betray indif- ference or a hackneyed observance of form, ren- der the last offices to the deceased; • and a hired sill smelling Of its last inmate, bears the body to the grave from which, perhaps, the bones of some old tenant Of the 'sod are dis- played, to make room for the uew one, destined in process of time to a similar ejectment. Here, the deceased soldier is borne to his last resting-place on the shoulders of his comrades; the gag under which he fought and died is the pall which covers his remains; the sword and other emblems of his profession, which surmount the body, speak more than the mO4 eloquent funeV, oration to the heart of tb.e. rpeLtSP ; the martial music, in solemn cadence, disposes the soul to suitable emotions ; the fresh grave, open to receive its first offering; the short but affecting ritual is pronounced by the, lips of tt brother soldier, perhaps in the faltering accents faf friendship; and the last volley seems to announce the entrance of the immortal part into the portals of eternity.—Twelve Years' Military Adienlatres.

ITALIAN TYIIANIZT.—AII that Gian Maria Vis- conti preserved of sovereign power was an un- bounded indulgence in every vice. Ms libertinism would hardly have been remarked; he was chiefly signalised by the frightful pleasure which he sought in the practice of cruelty. He was passionately devoted to the chase, but such sports soon failed to quench his thirst for cruelty. The torture inflicted on mute animals, not finding expression by speech, did not come up to his ferocious ideas of enjoyment, He therefore resolved to substitute men for brute animals, and caused all the criminals condemned by the tribunals to be given up to him as objects of this inhuman sport. He had his hounds fed with human flesh, in order to render them more ferocious In tearing their victims; and when ordinary con- victs were scarce, he denounced to the tribunals even the crimes in which he had participated, to obtain the condemnation of his accomplices; after which, he delivered them to his huntsman, Squarcia Giramo, charged with providing for the ducal chase. He was at last, on the 16th of May, 1412, assassin- ated by some Milanese nobles.—Sirneadi's Italian Republics. DEAFNESS OF THE AGED--Nothing is more common than to hear old people utter 'querulous complaints with regard to their increasing deaf- ness; but those who do so are not perhaps aware that this infirmity is the result of an express and wise arrangement of Providence in constructing the human body. The gradual loss of hearing is effected for the best purposes; it being te give ease and quietude to the decline of life, when any noises or sounds from without would but discompose the enfeebled mind, and prevent peaceful meditation. Indeed, the gradual withdrawal of all the sen,,es, and the perceptible decay of the frame, in old age, have been wisely ordained in order to wean the human mind from the concerns and pleasures of the world, and to induce a longing for a more per- fect state of existence. LOUIS XIV.—MADAME DE MAINTENON. The king lived in perpetual violation of every moral duty; but during his effective reign of 65 years', he never ate meat on a fast day but when ill, and never was absent a single day from mass but once, on a very long march of his army. Mad. de Maintenon accumulated all the outward means of human enjoy- ment. According to the estimate of the world, she was the most prosperous of women. But her own descriptions betray the difference between prosperity and happiness. In looking into a iirz h poiia at. Manly, she said to a friend, "You see how hingt:id the carp are. They are like me: they regrei, heir mud." "What a punishment," she often e.‘:cl.-ileled, "It is to have to amuse a man who is no berger amuse- able r— Ed/alai/0 Review. A CURIOUS CASE OF HOMICIDJI

One of the most remarkable physicians of bit day and generation was Andreas Vesalius, who nourished in the 16th century. He was physician. in-chief to Charles V., and afterwards to his son, Philip. ~ Some of the stories told of his wonderful powers are questionable, to say the least, while Others are well autl.entieated. He died on his return from the Holy Land, having been cast by a storm upon the barren desert island of Zanthe. The occasion of his voyage to Jerusalem is the sub- ject..of the story. A Spanish nobleman, of considerable wealth and political influence, was taken dangeronsy sick, and Vesalius was called to attend him. He came, and found the nobleman, as he believed, breathing his last. All known restoratives were resorted to, but without avail. The patient was pronounced dead, beyond the power of mortal aid to help him. The question arose among the man's friends— and he had many of them—What had been the matter with him? And probably no one was more . anxious to know than was the physician himself. At length he suggested that the body should be opened, for a post•mortem examination, to which the friends consented. One or two of the near relatives were opposed, but they were overruled, and gave in. Accordingly, on the second day after the sup- poseldeath, Vesalius, with one or two assistants, set at work upon the operation. The breast was Lid open, and though there was a slight show of blood, the physician did not yet dream of what he was to find. Upon lifting the sternum, he was horrified at finding a flow of warm blood, and see- ing a distinct pulsation of the heart. It had been a case—a wonderful case--of suspended anima- tion. But the man was dead now beyond human aid. Dead, surely The friends of the defunct nobleman heard of the case, and cane down upon the unfortunate doctor most vengefully. They not only accused him of murder before the civil court, but also accused him of impiety l'efore the Holy Inquisition', hoping that he might be burned at the stake by that awful tribunal. The civil court found no bill against him; but the officers of the Inquisition would have con- signed him to a terrible punishment had not thi king, partly by authority, and partly by prayerful entreaty, obtained his acquittal, on condition, how- ever, that ha should expiate his crime by a pilgrim- age to the Holy Land, clad in pilgrim's weeds, with sandals, staff, and scrip. He went, and it was on his return that he lost his life, as we have told. 8.0.

div.head: SAMMY'S WAGER.
div.p: SAMMY'S WAGER.

Our little Irrepressible—he will be four years eld come next June—came into the house the other day with his pinafore off and thrown away, and his clothing otherwise demoralized, and hailed the maid with f "Ho I Biddy, I tan jam\p higher zan 'e big pump out in e' yard." "o—go away wild you. What d'you mane by that, Sammy 'I" "I tell 'oo I tan jump higher zan'e pump. Now 1

And he caught Bridget by the dress' and pulled her away out into the yard, where stood the old wooden pump, insisting upon it that he could jump higher than that pump. "There," said the girl,—" now let'e see you jump." "Ho ! Biddy, if I do it, lb 'oo die' me a tam- berry tart '!" Yes.—Bridget promised him, if he would jump higher than the pump, that he should have a cran- berry tart. Then the little hero clambered up on to the platform and gave a tremendous jump— jumped with all his might and main. And then, with a comical leer, and a defiant nod at the pump, he cried out:

"Ho ! now, old pump, 'et 's see 'oo jump !" And he clapped his chubby hands in high glee when the old thing utterly refused to bulge. The pump couldn't jump a bit! And then Biddy saw where she had been sold. However, Sammy was her favourite; and she took him in and washed him, and put on his pinafore, and gave him the promised tart. 8. 0.

I have heard the anecdote related of different in- dividuals, but I think .the Poet Burns was the true hero of the cutting remark involved. A number of friends had assembled at an inn in Dumfries, the poet brjnf of the party, and in course of conversa- tion allualori wes made to a man who had died only the day before—a man well-known in that region, and one universally respected and es- teemed. •

" ! that reminds me," said a man of the com- pany, more noted for his avarice and double-dealing than for any moral qualities, "I must attend the (uneral, and I have . not a black coat to my back. Burns lam about your size; can you not laud me a black coat ?"

The man's Imesence was distasteful, if not dis- gusting in the poet, at any rate and to be thus applied to by him aroused his inflignation though he did not manifest it by any show of id-feeling. His reply, however, was significant: "Sir, I intend to be present at the funeral my- self, and I have but one black coat, I am, of course, unable to grant your request. I cannot lend you my sables, but I can recommend to you a perfect substitute. Just throw your character over your shoulders and your mantle will be black enough, Heaven knows 1" s. O.

div.head: COMFORTS OF THE POOR.
div.p: COMFORTS OF THE POOR.

The poor man has his wife and children about him—and what has the rich man more? lie has the same enjoyment of their society the same solicitude for their welfare, the same pleasure in their good qualities, improvement, and success ; their connection with him is as strict and intimate, their attachment as strong, their gratitude as warm. I have no propensity to envy any one, least of all the rich and great ; but if I were dis- posed to this weakness, the subject of my envy would be a healthy young man, in full possession of his strength and faculties, going forth in a morning to work for his wife and children, or bringing them home his wages at night.

EDMUND BURRS'S passion for the poetry on Virgil is significant. His early devotion to Edward Young, the grandiose author of the "Night Thoughts," is not to be wondered ht, though the inspiration of the youthful Burke, either as poet or critic, may be questioned when we find him rapturously scribbling in the margin of his copy— " Jove claimed the verse old Romer sung, But God himself inspired Dr Young."
But a boy's enthusiasm for a favourite Poet is a thing to rejoice over. The years that bring the philosophic mind will not bring--they must bud— enthusiasm.

•Tax air of the sea taken at a great distance from land, or even on the shore and in ports when the wind blows from the open, is in an almost perfect state of purity. Near continents the land winds drive before them en atmosphere always impure, but at a distance from the coasts this impurity has disappeared. The sea rapidly purifies the pesti- lential atmosphere of continents; hence every expanse of water of a certain breadth becomes an absolute obstacle to the propagation of epidemics. THE reserved man possesses strong affections and warm sympathies, may hold his convictions with fervour and his principles with enthusiasm; at any- rate no one has the right to assume that he does not simply because he does not hasten to proclaim the fact. Reserve, indeed, implies that there is something to reserve, and we may well wait with modesty to discover what it is that our reserved friend thinks it advisable to keep back before he is charged with coldness or insensibility. COTTON is not a fibre, but a plant hair. It bolds to be spun into a thread because of peculiar twists in each hair, shown under the microscope, espe- cially in polarised light. Linen thread may be spun because the flax fibres have certain roughilesses on their surface, which enable them to cling together. Hence it is impossible to make as Ewe linen ELS cot- ton cloth, but it is ;ouch stronger.

THE HEALTH OF WARRINGTON.

Sir,—lt seems to me that, at last, our sanitary autho- rities are doing what ordinary common sense would have led them to do atfirst.: viz., utilize and adapt pre- mises already existing as a temporary hospital for small- pox. It is the proud distinction and characteristic of Warrington officialdom to do differently iu such matters from the way in which other people would act. Fancy meeting a sudden outburst of smallpox with the remedy of a new hospital which, !although of iron, would take seeks to erect Is not that sublime? I think it is time that Warrington people began to ask very strenuously why it is that the town is so frequently plagued by epidemic disease? Has the much vaunted pail system, so dear to the heart of one of our distin- guished citizens, anything to do with it? I believe it .is, and must have of necesity. Further more, why are not the known insanitary regions of this townj dealt with? Is it, or is it not the case, that time Borough Medical Officer and the Borough surveyor were, months ago, instructed to institute in- quiries and prepare a report concerning at least one of these insanitary areas? If such was the case, was that instruction carried out? If it was, where and what is the report ? If the report condemned the area, why is nothing done? These are inquiries, sir, which through you I respect- fully press upon the ratepayers of Warrington, and upon all who feel an interest in the sanitation of the town. In my judgment, we are entitled to put all manner of reasemnable and earnest pressure upon our officials. They may work hard, but they will have to work harder yet, and they need to be encouraged to do their duty with- out fear or favour from anybody.—Yours faithfully, JOHN YONGE. 13, Wilson Patten-st., Sept. 14, 1892.

THE LICENSING QUESTION AT WAR- RINGTON. Sir,—The action of the magistrates at the last Brews- ter Sessions, leads me to doubt if it is possible to get anything like justice to anybody except the favoured Brewery Company. I think it will be a scandal and a Shame if six of Messrs. Greenall tenants should be turned out of their houses and done out of their living, by having their licenses taken away without the slightest consideration being given to the tenants of the licensed houses that are proposed to be given up. People who have paid considerable sums in the shape of goodwill, or bonus, and invested their hard-earned savings in the shone of trade furniture, utensils, acc., will find their stock to be of little or no value at the closing of their houses. Bow ready Brewery Companys, Ric., were to talk of justice and compensation during the I ..te Government when the endowment scheme was en the tapis. The first people to forg2t compensation now are the class of monopolists who would have reaped so much benefit from it had the law been passed as they ex- pected. It must be rather hard to be deprived of one's living because they want to improve their revenues by transferring their licenses into somebody else's district. As Conservatives, they worked hard at the last election, and now we find the men who should stand by them being drummed up to confirm the greatest mistake that has ever been made in Warrington. It will be a scandal and a shame if any bcdy of gentlemen occupy- ing the poeition of magistrate, should allow themselves to be the nominees of a Brewery Company. Next Tues- day may prove to the community who these gentlemen are; and I hope the public at large will take notice of tbera.—Yours,
CITIZEN.

STINKING WATERS AROUND WARRINGTON. Sir,—ln your " Things Heard, &c." attention is drawn to the condition of the Mersey, thus " that part of the Mersey that flows through Warrington has of late been stinking abominably." This is so ; and I am sorry to say it is very often the case. It is further said, " talk about the fish forsaking the Mersey on account of its pollution, lam surprised the birds do not forsake the air above it—it is so polluted sometimes." I have been in the habit of walking round Arpley on the river hank for fifteen years, and am satis- fied that many birds that used to be seen there have for- saken it. Some time ago it used to be a pleasure to walk from Atherton's Quay round Arpley to Warrington Bridge, and from that Bridge to the Locks at Padding- ton, iistening meanwhile to the music of the birds and looking at the flowing water. But, alas,those days are gone. Beneath Longford Bridge flows another filthy stream ; that it stinks is too true. Turning towards Dallam you shortly come to Sankey Brook, which flows through the meadows to Bewsey, and from thence alongside of the canal, both giving, a sickening stink. When you arrive at the old mill near Buttermilk Bridge, by the ditch along the "walk side" to the canal, you see a quagmire of -filth. The Fight, and the odour arising therefrom are offensive in the extreme. These waters pass Sankey Bridges to the river Mersey, so that Warrington is three parts surrounded by filthy waters. The County Couucil would do us a kindness if they (or the Rural Sanitary Authority) would take steps to remedy the evil. Though we cannot expect to fish there as of yore, yet to see clean water would be a boon.—Yours, &c., Warrington, Sept. 14th, 1892.
E. G.

THEEBAW AND DIGNIJM ON EVOLUTION. Sir,—The above significent conjunction must surely be productive of serious consequences to Spencerian Philos- ophy, if indeed it does not effectually restore the Chaldean legend of creation. I mean no disrespect to Mr. Dignum in thus coupling him with an anonymous scrib- bler, who,like a literary moonlighter,fires his blunderbuss from behind the cowardly covert of a pen-name. This noble controversialist—not having the courage of his opinions—thus avoids the unpleasant contingency of being held up to public ridicule as an ignorant inter- -meddler in things beyond his grasp. This monument of erudition accuses me of "knowing everything." But the" untutored savage" has taught me one thing, viz., upon how slender a provocation ani with what absolute ignorance of the matter in hand some indiscretes will rush into print. Mark what this intellectually " naked barbarian ', says :—" I should have thought that, according to evolution, all forms, whether extinct or extant were merely transitional." After this no one, who has the slightest knowledge of the subject, will accuse " Thee- baw " of an encyclopcechc knowledge of geology and evolution ! He "should nave thought" more about the matter and learnt that some forms am persistent through all the ages, from their first appe:trance—notably Littgula which has existed from Silurian times and is still extant. I rhould not have deemed this babbler worthy of notice, but that he, in his ignorance, adds force to what I have to say as to Mr. John Dignum's missapplied knowledge of the subject. Both, the savage and the savant, illustrate the fact that, in their opinion the mere accumulation of fact and observation of phenomena may be innocent and allowable, but. the Inoment anyone begins to apply the knowledge so gaped —showing its inconsistency with some traditional belief—that moment they are on the " rampage," attacking their c poonent by screaming atheistic theory, &c. This is the treatment everybody has been subjected to who has tried to shovr that natural pheno- mena were the result of natural law. The Newtons, the Galileos, the Darwins and the Huxle-, s have, and always must, go through this experience at the hands of the Dignums of their time ;probably ass chastening inflicted for their sins. But the world still moves, and the sun of science refuses to stand over the valley of debate while the zealots scream their enemies to death or to deafness. Mr. Dignutn in his wrath forgets that it is not with his little book, in which these traditional views End suit- able entombment, hut with the summary which was published and so likely to be read by the public. That summary Mr. Dignum has endorsed, and it contains statements which are not true. Hence my objection. Poor old Archreopteryx ! at this time of life to be called a monstrosity ! Thou art indeed an inconvenient diet ; and, if vituperation would dispose of thee, thy silent testimony would be disregateled. But what in nature is

a monstrosity? Is this not a word like "freak of nature" and . "nature's abhorrence of a vacuum"— phrases invented merely to conceal our want of know- ledge of the laws upon which these phenomena depend? Has my friend reflected upon the high improbability of the finding of even one specimen of a single " monstro- strosity ? ' Mr. Dignum's monstrosity must have been one of a large family, the other members of which the imperfectiou of the geultlica4 record has not yet revealed to us.

Finally, I am as fully convinced as to the existence of a great First Cause as Mr. Dignura himself; but I am not so confident as to his ways of working. lam not in receipt of private inforreation on this point; and I know no source of information, written or oral, so reliable as the logical deductions from the observations of nature. But these methods may well not commend themselves to men who regard Haeckel and Strauss as in "the outer darkness of fools." To call a man a fool is not to convict hiss of folly, but yourself of intemper- ance.—l am, &c., Cardiff, Sept. 11th, 1892.
JOHN PEERS.
LICENSING JUSTICNI AT WARRINGTON.

Sir,—Surely a just rebuke against those who ought to justly administer the laws of the land, was never more called for, than in the case that has now aroused the deep sense of indignation of the most thoughtful and loyal people of Warrington, against the decision of the Lieensing Committee, on the 25th of last month. In 1888 they committed a similar, but, somewhat less blunder, than they have at present. On that occasion, the full bench of magistrates were equal to the case, and, wisely overthrew the efforts of the brewers and the Licensing Committee to increase the drinking facilities of this pitiable drink-cursed town. We hope and pray, that on September 20th, they will again come to the rescue, and frustrate the cunning ends of the sordid, heartless, lovers of gain from the ruinous drink traffic.

Sir, you truly remarked in your issue of September 29th, 1888, " The Licensing Committee of the borough of Warrington have made the discovery that they neither repr:iented the views of the public, nor of their brother magistrates, when they took steps to increase the facilities for obtaining intoxicating liquors." On finding they had taken a wrong course on that occasion, they resolved to amend their ways the following year. , But their commendable efforts were frustrated by the not ' over commendable failure of the Magistrates' Clerk to give due notice of objection to houses complained of. Last year it was generally understood that the Bench were going to take action o'n the same lines ; taking due care that their servant the clerk timely did his part in the matter. But alas ! public expectations were tills-placed. They actually proved them to be not needed, as well as of little gain t 3 the owners thereof ; as shown by their repeated offers to give them up as soon as they could cunningly beguile the magistrates into an exchange so as to improve the social and moral conditions of the in- habitants as well as the value of the property in the neighbourhoods of Bewsey and Battersby-lane, by allow- ing other houses to be provided there! Further, their Worships must not forget that in his great wisdom one of their brethren in May last, made a lasting impression on the people and press of England, by his remarkable definition of a drunken person, viz., "To be drunk was to be in such a condition as to ren- der it impossible that anybody could pass that person without seeing at once that that person was drunk." Their conduct cannot fail to bring the magistrates into public condemnation, and will, I trust, hasten the time when the people shall have absolute control in settling the question of how many licenses shall be granted. The time is at hand. Some magistrates don't see, won't see, that anything but highest and best results can arise, by their increasing the number of gin palaces in the Bewsey district, and in the more-to-be dreaded district of Battersby-lane, so near the barracks. Neither do they seem to think that the public generally are justly dis- pleased at the manner in which they bow their necks to the galling yoke of the t3wn's worst foes—brewers and publicans. .

Why, in the name of common-sense, should licenses be multiplied either in Bewsey or Battersby-lane, by giving two new licenses to Greensll, Whitley and Co., who have not a brick on the spot nor a license? And why not, instead of multiplying licenses in Bat- tersby-lane, if a full license must be placed there in direct opposition to the protest of the property owners, and inhabitants, (nearly every householder of whom, only a year or two since signed a petition against any such thing being put there) grant the license to Mr. Bol- ton and thereby prevent two drink shops being next door to each other, as is the case now in Buttermarket-st., &c. But there is an unenviable responsibility in making these places as bad if not much worse than Butterrnarket- street, with drunkenness and immortality. In conclusion, the brewers and their friends know full well that they must use all the means they alone are capable of, to beguile their friends on the Bench now. For all their chances of doing so and getting licenses in a respectable neighbourhoods are very small in the future. Be up and doing ye true loves of justice, and of mankind! As Emerson soundly teaches :--- " Whoever fights, whoever falls, Justice conquers ev-rmore. Justice after as before ; And he who battles on her side, God, though he were ten times slain, Crowns him victor glorified, Victor over death and pain For ever." Yours faithfully, R. STOREY. Warrington, Sept. 7th 1892.

div.head: EAUR ORDEItLY (!) ROOM.
div.p: EAUR ORDEItLY (!) ROOM.

We'n an Orderly Room i'th' owd village, Wheer th' country's defendere aw meet ; An' to hear um debatin' on prizes, Is moor then a ey'ry-day treat. They're ez quiet ez lambs i' a wolf walk, Till thay'n sleckent wi' "Barleycorn John ;" Wen the gain' then begins wi' a vengeance, An' they're aw on ther legs, to a mon ! We'll suppose ez they're met after shootin', Wen the prizes are given away; Then the chaps wi' the gift o' the gab start, An' oh I tiler's the " divil to play !" The Sargunt, a stalwert defender, Makes speeches wi' ev'ry chap's prize ; But a Corporal, quite nauf seas ovver, Interrupts him an' blesses his eyes Yo may pictur' yersels, wot a hubbub Is goin' abeawt aw the time ; An' the langwidge that sum on um uses, Is moor than grand, its sublime ! No parson cull ever cum nigh it, No bishop cud speyk hafe as weel ; It's a mixture o' boarditeskoo lingo, An' anythin' else that's genteel (I) It's smaw wunder the Sarjunt gets shirty, Wen his speeches are knockt upo' th' yed ; An' he wishes that raw yedded Corporal Wuz safely teed up in his bed. He cud then ger slung wi' his bizness, An' free fro that osciffer's tung, Wud be able to do aw that's needed, VVitheaut takkin' measures that's strung. But it wuzn't to be, so the Sarjunt, ' In tones booed) sharp an' severe, Bellow'd eawt, " Tak' that chap to the Guard Room, An' put him i' mannicles theer ! Wile aw owd my glorious commission, Fer sarvin' my country's greyt cause, Aw'll stond no darn'd nonsense fro' nob'dy, Thet caunt keep his tung in his jaws!" Ov coorse, ther's an eend cams to aw things, An' the finish war pleasant to this; Fer the Corporal, quickly repentin', Confess'd ez he'd done mitch amiss. Wi' his gizzert wi' sorrow o'erflowin', An' his ee'n lookin' waery an' full ; Like o mon, he begg'd pardon o' th' Sarjunt, ' An they petch'd it aw up at " 'The Bull !" TUM O'PEGS. Nyowt-in God bless o', Sept. 9,1892.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

The" Bullionist " says : The Manchester Town Coun- cil, having by this time discovered that ship canal estimates and statements are liable to error, have de- cided to have an independent report from independent engineers. The cry at the Council meeting on Wednes- day was the old" We have been misled all along." But surely these gentlemen will scarcely repeat the excuse after this ; and yet an independent report on the finan- cial position is as requisite as one on the engineering position. It is now perfectly clear that neither Lord Egerton's million and a-half, nor the two millions men- tioned in the same breath, will see the end of things. , Interest will be piled up, for it is now said on good , authority that the completion will be nearer the end of 1894 than 1893, and there are claims, and errors in estimating assets, which will bring the money wanted to probably three millions at least.

div.head: DOW c BY THE SEA.
div.p: DOW c BY THE SEA.
[WITHOUT TIER BASSINETTE.]
BY JOHN PEERS.

In emulation of the now historic individual who had such a spree, down by the sea, with sixteen kids and a bassinette, I shook off the dust—nay it was raining—say mud—of Penketh, and took my hook by a Cook ticket from Bank Quay to Cardiff The state of the weather at starting gives no excuse for whatever of dryness may be found in this vera- cious narrative. No, the rain came down—by the way i never saw it going up—but in this case it was coming down in a silent steady drizzle as though it meant it. This was nice weather to get up at three o'clock in the morning to welcome. Plea- sure ! there are more pains taken in thy name than in the pursuit of much good. There, that is a moral reflection which should compensate for the mud. After the usual delay incident to excursions we were away, but not before I had delighted mine -eyes, and, let us hope, chastened .my spirit and humbled my pride, by a perusal of your correspond- ence columns. For this was on Saturday morning last at 7 a.m. The start was timed 7.30, but only effected at 7.49 giving us plenty of time to settle down in our places, learn some little of each other's history, and admire what we could see out of the carriage windows. I believe we did get away at last, as I am here sitting in Cardiff on this good Sunday afternoon, intent upon telling your readers all the " moving incidents of flood and field " which befell your very Special Correspondent. Yes, now I remember, we changed at Chester, and had not much more than an hour to wait. Some of us felt growing old —many :ha a out-grown their patience when a train came, in which we were allowed to pack ourselves , away much as the herrings are in a barrel, barrin— the salt. But after all the inconveniences, it is a glorious mode of travelling when compared with: that of the old stage coach. The rapid change of scenery is delightful, the soft undulations of our , dear old Cheshire into the well-wooded midlands, ' with their fruit trees laden with golden treasures. Now across some river-made flat alluvial marshes, along the verge of some winding stream or moun- tain torrent; panting up some steep ascent or rush- ing like an avalanche down some well-graded de- clivity. As we got on we changed passengers and took on a contingent of native Welsh—who were not only Welsh, but spoke it very much and very fast. Now,l have no objection to anyone speaking Welsh if they will do it quietly—say in the miscrophonic But let me not be disrespectful to the language of mine ancestors—those ancient lords of the soil— peers of the realm, who roamed over the country in their uniforms of blue—well woaded. One old lady who rejoiced in the not uncommon cognomen of Jones, which seems to agree with her, would not have her small impediments, consisting of a hamper of live fowls, a tin trunk, a basket and a few other little trifles, such as elderly females of her class often affect—these she would not let out of her sight, rejecting the suggested guard's van with in- dignation. No ! she preferred to have them on our knees and toes. She would have them shifted every five minutes to make sure that none of us had pocketed them while she looked out of the windows. But even she found peace at last in devouring the contents of a large basket of provisions and talking Welsh ,with a mouthful of bread arid butter. Now, I should think this must enhance the difficulty of uttering this difficult-looking language very materially. How such a word as Llanprwlrch could get round such an obstruction is a marvel to me; but this is nothing to the feats of orality that were performed on that occasion. When some three quarters of the journey had been got over a mild-looking member of the female persuasion got into our apartment, and after a labial salute to her male convoy took her seat opposite me and occupied herself in arranging a lot of books, papers, and pamplileta she had brought with her. By and by, how- ever, she begged my next neighbour to exchange places with her, and down she plumps by my side. Oh ! my ! Here was a nice situation for a married man and the father of a family! And the train going at 40 miles an hour, and no communication with the guard. What was the woman going to do! Well, I screwed up my courage to the sticking point, made a determined effort at self-restraint, and sat still awaiting further develop- ments. They came! She drew forth a book, and be- gan to read it in such a position that I also could do the same. It was the memoir of Pastor C.H.Spurgeon. I therein and thereby learned more about that great and good man than I ever expected, wished, or wanted to know; as well as that of his father and grandfather. But all things must have an end—even the life of 'so good a man, and then she began the serious work of her mission. She drew forth one by one those terrible offensive missiles,known as tracts. Now I am as intractable in this matter as Huxley himself. But she did not offer me one. Still, after my natural trepidation had somewhat abated, and I could use what little courage had not oozed out from my finger ends, she, after some few general : remarks, asked me " At what age did I think a young child would receive the blessing of the ; Lord"! Now, I could not have been more flaber- , gasted had ste asked me for some difficult. algebraic solution. such as the contents three times seven ! What a situation ! She had actuaily taken me—not thank Heaven, for better or worse—but for no better or worse than a sky-pilot ! A peri- patetic Sti,ggins on tour ! Great goodness! What is it that has led to this dreadful mistake ! Was it this hat ? or these goggles that an un- happy fate compels me to wear? Or was it that general " Heaven bless you my child " ! look which same of my critics have failed tc detect in me ? Do I, oh do I look like a journyman curate out on strike? No !it must be that hat. It is a borrowed hat—it is not mine. It was left in my care by a favousite cousin of mine, BO I am just wearing it to keep the moths out. Here is an ex- ample how kind actions do lead people into trouble. Well, having staved off this appalling question as well as I could, and listened very patiently to a dis- sertation on the blessings wrought by seaside preaching, and confessed to never having seen or heard any of her favourite preachers, I took advan- tage of a lull to gently tell her that I was one of. those unfortunates who had lost what she thought so precious. Strange indeed are the social associa- tions of this world. Here were two folk for gather- ing together than whom perhaps no more opposite Coal Ibe found. Both lam certain perfectly con- scientious; but how differently so. She, good soul, abhorred reason and reasoning as destructive of belief and the good influence of" the word." I cherish reason as the best and most glorious of our , gifts. However, we parted with mutual good-will, . good wishes, and respect..

Well, Cardiff was Jiained at last—about half-past three, and, after securing a roost and a ramble, I sought the recumbent, a not unreasonable thing to do after seventeen hours of the other position. But it is dark and post time, so no more &c., &c., until next week, when I may—if I may—carry my ad- ventures a stage further. (To be Continued.)

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 17, 1892. WESLEYAN BAZAAR AT WAIIRINGTON.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 17, 1892. WESLEYAN BAZAAR AT WAIIRINGTON.

On Tuesday afternoon a bazaar was opened in Bold-st. Wesleyan Schoolroom in aid of the funds for renos ating, relighting and heating Bold-st. Chapel. The bazaar was opened by Mr. W. Barlow, of Warrington, in the presence of a large gathering of visitors. Amongst those present were the Revs. J. E. Kirtlan (who presided), J. Gunnell, A. Free- man, and T. Ross; Dr. S. Smith, Messrs. R. Garnett, S. B. Stringer. P. Silcock,Brown(Lymm),L l'igot, A. Horrocks, Lawton, and others. The s.choolroom had been very prettily decorated for the occasion, and the stalls were well laden with a fine and varied display of goods. There were six stalls, in all, including a young man's stall and a refreshment stall. They were presided over by the following ladies:—jr, S. B. Stringer, Mrs. Kirtlan, Mrs. Gunnell, Mrs. T. Starkey Smith, Mrs. Alfred Silcock, the Misses Bradbury, Miss Laverock, the Misses Gleave, Mrs. Jubb, M. W. Silcock, Mrs. Ross, Miss Benson, Miss Blackhurst, Mrs. Bodle, Mrs. Taylor, Mrs. G. Weaver, Mrs. Chorley, , Mrs. Gandy, Mrs. Barlow, Mrs. White, Mrs. Nicholson, Mrs. Belford. Mrs. Allan, and Miss G. Nicholson. The refreshment stall was in charge of Miss Weaver, and Miss Lawton .; and the flower stall was presided over by Miss Beaman, Misses Craik, assisted by Miss Silcock and Miss Taylor. A leading feature of the decoration was an imitation of a waterfall which had been designed and carried out on the platform by Mr. F. J. Dell. It was a capital piece of work, and a profusion of handsome plants that had been used gaveit a very realistic appear- ance. The water was conveyed in pipes from the mains and its constant trickle added a music of its own to the proceedings. The room was decorated in other ways by means of small various coloured banners. The bazaar, it should be explained, had been so far as the preparation of articles of sale went for the most part got up by the ladies connected with Bold-st. chapel, who had been engaged in the work for a considerable time P be said that the display which waas, stmaanddeitantltahy truly was highly creditable to them. There were in addition, the committees which had charge of the various department. The conveners of these committees were the following gentlemen ;—Pub- lishinr, committee, Mr. W. Silcock; amusement commit- tee, "Mr. S. B. Stringer ; musical committee, Mr. Fanshawe ; and decoration committee, Mr. P. Silcpck. The special attractions of the bazaar included music, ventriloquial sketches, lantern exhibitions, and a museum of curiosities. This museum included many i interesting objects. There was an interesting collection of articles from the Soudan, lent by Major Mckie, and two very fine pictures were on view having been sent 'by Mr. Cherley. Sergeant Bodle's medals were also dis— played, and amongst other contributors to this depart ment were Mr. Dutton, Mr. Pigot, Mr. Prince, and others. During the evening amusing ventriloquial I sketches were given by Mr. Grounds, of Latchford. At I the opening The CHAIRMAN said he should like to impress upon the ; minds of their friends, if they needed to be impressed, that that was altogether a religious effort, and that they wanted that effort to be baptised by the spirit of their religion at the very commencement of it. He had known much about bazaars, and he had known sonic things which he had not cared much about, but he believed that, of late years, bazaars had been conducted on much better principles than they were some five and twenty years ago. Be had no doubt at all that their friends there were all anxious to do that which was best for the cause with which they were associated, and to bring glory to God. That was their object in all their efforts of that kind. The Rev. T. Ross then teed a portion of scripture, after which 'The Rev. A. FIZEEMAN said he knew that Mr. Barlow did not require much introduction to a Warrington audience. In connection with Bold-street Chapel, he had long held the office of treasurer, and he had in many ways interested himself in the welfare of the chapel. Like himself, Mr. Barlow could not lay claim to having been born in Warrington, but, of course, they could not all claim anythingso marked in the way of distinction as that. For many years, Mr. Barlow, had resided in the town, and had shown a deep and constant interest, especially in the chapel trust. He (Mr. Freeman) was glad for one that M. Barlow's services had been secured for the opening of that bazaar. (Hear, hear.) Mr. W. BARLOW, in declaring the bazaar open, said that, as many of them were aware, the Committee that had the management of that bazaar nsade application in various directions to secure some gentleman of influence to perform what he was about to do. He regretted very much that they were riot successful, because they should have been very much pleased had they had some stranger there, to gracefully open the bazaar besides giving them some small pecuni- ary help. He was very glad to do anything he could to assist the cause there and to show his sympathy with the , ladies who had done such a grand work. They wanted to raise £BOO by that effort. It seemed a large sum but he hoped that when the bazaar cicsed they should not fail in having that amount. The chapel adjoining was in a nirty state and required renovating, decorating and cleaning thoroughly. It had not been done for many years. The lighting of the chapel was also defective, and, altogether, they could not do with less than the amount he had named. He then declared the bazaar open. Mr. TAYLOR, in moving a vote of thanks, to Mr. Barlow said that gentleman had given a handsome Con- tribution towards the bazaar fund. Dr. S. SMITH seconded the vote of thanks which was heartily accorded. ' The Rev. T. Ross said that Mr. R. Pierpoint, the mem- ber for the borough, had sent a very kind nets saying absence from home did not permit of his being there that day. Ho would, however, send them a guinea. (Applause.) Councillor J. Fairclough and Alderman , Harrison had also sent notes saying they were sorry that they would not be able to be present with them. WEDNESDAY. The bazaar was again formally opened on Wednesday. The Rev. A. Freeman presided, and in the absence of Dr. Starkey Smith, who was expected to declare the bazaar 1 open, Mr. Taylor performed that office. The CHAIRMAN explained that Dr. Smith was prevented from attending by the calls of business. He also referred to the great services and generous gifts which Dr. Smith had given to Bold-st., chapel. Mr, Taylor in declaring the bszaar open. said that Dr. Smith had been a very generous contributor towards that bazaar. He had sent a cheque for £4O with the intimation that Mrs. Smith would spend another £lO. (Applause.) He added that Mr. Barlow who opened the bazaar on the previous day, had given a contribution of £25, and that they had also received several gifts of £lO. Including these donations the total receipts of the previous day amounted to £287. —The Rev, J. GUNNELL moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Taylor for opening the bazaar. He said that although Mr. Taylor had made no allusions to his own gifts he had been a very liberal supporter of the bazaar.—Mr. Barlow seconded the vote of thanks which was heartily accorded. Mr. Taylor suitably responded, and after- wards the sales were proceeded with. On Thursday the bazaar was re-opened by Miss 18. Dutton, who gave a short and admirable address on the occasion. The takings of the bazaar up to closing time on Thursday night, amounted to £479 2s. 91d. The amount taken on Tuesday, was £272 es. 4d. ; on Wed- nesday, £ll5 7s. Id. ; and on Thursday, £9l 93. 40. The bazaar was open again last evening.

div.head: MARRIAGE AT ST.-_ MARY'S CATHOLIC
div.p: MARRIAGE AT ST.-_ MARY'S CATHOLIC
CHUltell.

On Thursday morning the marriage of Miss Eckersley, daughter of the late Mr. Joseph Bolters- ley. of Bridge-st., to Mr. Alfred Marsh, eldest son of Mr. James Marsh, of Rolleston-st., took place at St. Mary's Catholic Church, Buttermarket-st. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. Father Sumner, assisted .by the Rev. Father Duggan, Mr. Mather presiding at the organ. The bride, who was given away by her brother, Mr. John Eckersley was dressed in grey cashmere,trimmed with silk and embroidery, with a grey hat, trimmed with white velvet and feathers,and carrie4 a beautiful bouquet. The bridesmaids were Miss Mary Eckersley. Miss Alice Eckersley, sinters of the bride, and Miss Jane Brown, niece of the bridegroom, and each of them *ore a gold broach, gift of the bridegroom, helio- trope dresses, and fawn hats, and carried bouquets composed of pink roses and maidenhair fern. The groomsmen were Mr. James Lingard (best man), nephew of the bridegroom and Messrs. W. Dilworth and J. W. Dilworth. The happy couple proceeded after the wedding to Llandudno.

ARABS PASHA ItS HAPUTALR. I The" Times of Ceylon" says :—". We learn that, prior to leaving Mr. Lipton's estates to-day, Arabi Pasha and his party were to be driven down to the Leymastotte factory, where the tea from the whole group of the Haputale estates is manufactured. They were after- wards to proceed in special coaches provided by Mr. Lipton, via Bandarawella, Attampitiya, and Wilson's Bungalow,to Nuwara Eliya,where a stay of a day or two was to be made. They were then to go on to Kandy, where they will visit, and probably remain a couple of days with the pashas who are living there, reach- ing Colombo on the I.6th. Mr. Lipton would appear to have struck ups great friendship with the exile, as he has invited him to make a periodical stay at his estates, both for the benefit of his own health and of that of any of the pashas who may care to accompany him. The body of a young lady, believed to be Mrs. Long, of 60, Hutton-road, Canonbury-square, London, was en Wednesday found on the Great Northern Railway, near High Barnet, under circumstances suggestive of suieida. Sir G. Trevelyau, addressing his conatituents in the Bridgeton Division Of Glasgow, said the happy experi- ence of the Scotch office had gone far towards solving inestiovis of Heine Rule, for it had proved that if Scot- land could do very well with a separate executive's°, too, could other parts of the country. • •

div.head: MUSIC AND DANCING LICENSING SESSIONS.
div.p: MUSIC AND DANCING LICENSING SESSIONS.

I By the Public Health Act Amendment Act, 1890, ' which was adopted by the Warrington Corporation some time since, it was provided that no house, room, garden, or other place, used for the sale Of lintoxicating liquor, should be used for public music, !singing, or dancing without being licenced for such ! purpose at a special session, the licensing sessions, or the adjourned licensing sessions. The licensing Committee of the magistrates on Thursday sat in special session for the purpose of hearing applications for such licenses. The magistrates were Aldermen Holmes (chairman), Chandley and Burgess ; Messrs. John Paircliough and P. Monks and Captain Ridg- way. Music licences only were applied for by Joseph Allison, Cemetery Inn ; Robert Anderton, Cross Keys ; William Bolton, Royal Exchange; James Cheadle, Swan Inn; Samuel Clare, King and Queen Padgate ; Henry Corney, King's Arms, Buttermarket-street ; Thomas Critchley, Higher Angel ; Elizabeth Earle, Fox Inn; : Martha Guy, Millstone Inn ; Thomas Halton, Lower ' Seven Stars; Joseph Horlock, Rope and Anchor ; F. 'Jones, Courier's Arms ; Ann Kershaw, Blue Bell v • Henry King, Crow Inn' Bridge-street ; James Lee, Red Lion, Winwick-road ; George Littlewood, Ring-o'-Bells ' • Maud Loy, Eagle and Child; Francis Massey, Roebuck Hotel ; H. A. Powell, Vulcan ; Elizabeth Rushworth, Rose and Crown ; John Sampson, Norton Lrms, Latchford ; Samuel Silcock, Bear's Paw ; James Thomas, Bank- stree ; Thomas Walsh, Crown and Sceptre, Butteriaarket- street ; Peter White, Old Ball ; Mary Whittle, Marquis of Granby, Church-street; John Williamson, Golden Lion; Thomas Boscoe, Ring-o'-Bells, VVilderspool-road ; Martha Cook, Gardener's Arms, Brick-street ; George Crawford, Old House at Home, Friars' Green ; Walter Hewitt, Gladstone Arms ; Samuel Jones, Smith's Arms, Leigh- street ; Elizabeth Riley, Borough Arms ; J. Walsh, Strangers' Arms, Dial-street ; no objection being offered by the chief constable. Mr. A. Browne (appeared on behalf of the Warrington Licensed Victuallers' Associa- tion) and a large number of applicants. There were also applications for music and dancing licenses for the Patten Arms and the Lion Hotel.
THE WHITE MULL INN.-TIIE ENGAGEMENT Or PROBES•IIONAL
ARTISTES.

Mrs. Ann Balshaw applied for a music and dancing licence for the White Bull Inn, Buttermarket-strset, Mr. Browne said in this case the applicant desired to continue to engage professional talent for concerts at her house, but there could be no harm in engaging these professionals. There were sone 498 of these music ; licenses in Manchester in public-houses alone, and surely the magistrates would not say that these licenses should not be granted merely because of these professionals ' being engaged. Mrs. Balshaw allowed no females in the room where the entertainments took place, unless they were accompanied by their husbands, and no young boys, therefore there could be no objection. She did not want a licence for dancing except for step dancing, and he was doubtful whether it was necessary to have a license for this; and he thought it only required this where there was dancing by couples for the purpose of enjoyment.—The Magistrates' Clerk: Where music or dancing is subsidiary to something else and not sub- stantially the entertainment, license is not required. For songs after a dinner a license would not be required. —The Chief Constable said he most point u t that the landlady did not live on the premises, but out at Pad- gate.—Mr. Browne : She does not occupy the house there once a fortnight, to my personal knowledge.—The Chief Constable said for some years past persons of a very questionable character indeed, both male and female, had been employed at the inn, and they had. had considerable trouble in sending to the landlady Even now persons not belonging to Warrington, went there to perform and sing as to whom he had very grave doubts, and four persons who had been per- forming there a considerable time were convicted at that court for shop-lifting.

THIS HOP POLE INN. Joseph Coop, Hop Pole Inn, Horsemarket-et., applied through Mr. Browne, for a music and dancing license. Mr. Browne said Mr. Coop had occupied the house something like 18 months, and since he entered it he had greatly improved the place and the =duct of it. The license was for music and dancing for the concert room upstairs, also used for dinners, and the concert room downstairs. The applicant had five daughters, who managed the whole house. The concerts in the upper room were only held on Saturday nights. No boys were admitted, and no females unless accompanied by their husbands or friends. They would not have any " spitoon " artistes as they were called, and on one occa- sion had dismissed one of these after no kad sung ORO fng, a proof that he meant to conduct the house pro- perly by not allowing anything low there. He (Mr. Browne) thought the Chief Constable would say that the place had never been so well conducted as now.— Mr. Hunt said he had had no complaints about the house since Mr. Coop came into it. He had visited the house since, and found three or four of Mr. Coop's daughters there, highly respectable young women, who, he be- lieved would not countenance anything improper. There was nothing going on on Sunday nights in the concert rooms as there used to be. • THIS KING'S ARMS.

Henry Carney, King's Arms, Buttermarket-st.,applied for a music license. The Chief Constable said Mr. Carney conducted his house very well indeed. There was quite a transformation compared with what there used to be.

div.head: PATTEN ARMS AND NORTON ARMS.
div.p: PATTEN ARMS AND NORTON ARMS.

Mary E. Kiernan, Patten Arms, applied for a license for music and dancing.—Mr. Browne said the license was wanted in case of any private party being given and to allow of the piano being used in any room' John Sampson, Norton Arins, also applied for a musi. license only. lie stated he merely wanted it for a smok- ing concert twice a yeti% or so. ,

div.head: BEAR'S PAW INN.
div.p: BEAR'S PAW INN.

Samuel Si!cock, -lcw-,-I.iuttermarket-street, applied for a usic license.—The Chief-Constable : What about the barrel organ you have kicking up such a row ?—Mr. Silcock replied that he had had it removed.— The Chief-Cmstable : It disturbed the whole neighbour. hood.

div.head: LION HOTEL.
div.p: LION HOTEL.
Joseph Taylor, Lion Hotel, Winwick-road, applied for a music and dancing license.—Mr. Brown stated that the license was only wanted for the purpose of balls, and a dancing class there.
TWO HOUSES WITII A BAD ATMOSPIIHRR.

Eliza Young,. Shakespea.ra Inn, Dolman's-lane, made application for a music and dancing license.—The Chief-constable complained of the atmosphere of the house being had through it being too small and badly ventilated. When he went to it with Inspector Spinks, he was very glad to get out of it—George Crawford, the Old House at Home, Friars' Green, applied for a music and dancing license. The applicant said the license was only wanted so that anybody might play the flute who came in.—The Chief-constable said there was almost,the same atmosphere at this house as at the Shakespeare. It was only a question of a tin whistle, piccolo, or flute and an Irish jig, or a reel.

VULCAN INN. Henry A. -Powell applied for a music license for the Vulcan Inn, Dallam-lane. Mr. Browne represented the applicant. His client, he said, had a dancing class at the house, and taught the violin.—lnspector Spinks said neighbours/complained that a place formerly used as a skittle alley in the yard, behind the premises, which was used for the purposes in question was ruining the young men and young girls of the neighbourhood.
WORKMEN'S CLUB. Thomas Crompton applied for a music and dancing license for the Workmen's Club. Mr. Browne repre- sented him, and elicited the tact that no intoxicating drink was sold in the place.
CONSERVATIVE CLUB.
George Pilling, secretary for the Conservative Clnb, applied for a music and dancing license for that place.
COOPERATIVE FULLS.
Arthur H. Hat Untie. applied for licenses for the Co-operative Halls in Cairo-st., and Tanner's-lane.
TEIli DECISION.

The magistrates retired at a quarter to eleven to con- sider the applications. The only ones to which they then devoted any lengthened consideration were those of Mrs. Balshaw and Mr. Coop. They re- turned in an hour and five minutes and announced that they refused licenses in their cases, so far as dancing, and singing by professionals was concerned ; also that they refused in the cases of Wm. Bolton, James Cheadle, Henry King, Samuel tiilcock, James Thomas, Bank-st. ; Geo. Parker, Geo. Crawford, and Eliza Young. H. A. Powell was refused a license for dancing and granted one for music. All the other applications were acceded to.

div.head: MR. AND MRS. GLA.DSTONE.
div.p: MR. AND MRS. GLA.DSTONE.
VISIT TO NORTH WALES.

Sir Andr2w Clark has (says the "Daily Telegraph ") often tr:Tn heard to say that Mrs. Gladstone is quite as much entitled to the name r,f the Grand Old Woman as her husband is to that of the Grand Old Man. On Janu- ary 12th last Mrs. Gladstone's eightieth birthday came round, and she passed me morning in writing letters to her friends in England, a task which she accomplished without wearing glasses of any kind as aids to her sight. In fact, she has never yet known what it is to need spectacles, and her eyes are as bright as those of a young woman. Every morning passed by Mr. and Mrs. Glad- stone at Hawarden sees them both at church, nearly three-quarters of a mile away from the Castle, in the earls' morning. • Close to the church is the corrugated iron building in which Mr. Gladstone has already deposited about 20,000 volumes—the overflow of his own private library at the Castle—every volume of which he has placed with his own hand on the shelves of the new library which he has given to the parish of Hawarden. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstorie on Monday morning left Hawarden to spend a few days with Sir E. W. Watkin at his new chalet at the foot of Snovidon. The Premier broke his journey at Carnarvon in order to. receive an address from the kcal Liberal Associations. Ire the ourse of a short speech in reply to the address he said he was pleased to find that Wales, however occupied,

however absorbed at times she might have been with her own affairs, had not forgotten to speak a kindly word for Ireland. The Irish question she recognised as an urgent one, most truly consecreed by the remem- brance of former ages and of the terrible wrongs which for a length of time had been inflicted on the Irish people. The signal service which Wales had rendered ,to the cause of freedom had reached a point at which the establishment of strict religious equality would be I alike for the interest of all classes and denominations in the Principality and for the harmony of the country. For what she had done politically Wales had established a claim which was one of the strictest upon the consi- deration of the Liberal party, who, he hoped would not forget her. He, however, reminded the Welsh people that political changes were not to be effected at railway speed. The attainment even of the most signal triumphs at the elections must be followed by a period in which they would be called upon, indeed, for the viftue of a ceaseless energy, but in which they would also be called upon to display the virtue of a reasonable patience. He hoped that not even one session of Parliament would be allowed to pass without their being enabled to give some earnest to the people of Wales of their desire to deal with and, as far as they could, to promote and push for- ward the realization of their just demands. On Tuesday Mr. Gladstone visited Sir Edward Wat- kin's chalet on Snowdon, and was presented with an address by the Festiniog Liberal Association. The address referred to Home Rule for Ireland, Disestab- lishment and Disendowment of the English church in I Wales, the immediate necessity of dealing with the Welsh land question, and the need of a University to complete the educational edifice. Mr. Gladstone. in reply, said he trusted that the Parliament which they had chosen, ' and the Government which the sense of Parliament had recommended her Majesty to instal in office would do what was really expected of them, and would make all the progress that an intelligent and zealous course of effort would render possible towards meeting the wishes of Wales.

div.head: CLIMB UP SNOWDON.
div.p: A CLIMB UP SNOWDON.

I Wednesday was a finer day in Snowdonia than has been experienced for several days. Consequently the I excursionists to the top of Snowdon from every point of I the compass were far more numerous than usual. The expectations that Mr. Gladstone would make the ascent turned out to be not without foundation, though it was not completely accomplished. About eleven o'clock a party set out from the Chalet with the intention of as- cending either to top, or as far as Bwlchysaethan. This I party included Sir Edward and Lady Ingram Watkin, Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone, Mrs. Drew, Mrs. Edgar Watkin, and Mrs. Heenan. The assent to the end of the carriage road was leisurely made, Polly, the mettlesome cob of Sir E lward Watkin, drawing up the landau in which the ladies of the party took turns in riding. When the path commenced, Tommy, a sure-footed pony from the stables of the Goi...t Hotel, was called into requisition, Mrs. Gladstone riding for a considerable distance. Tommy, it should be stated, was the first pony that ever ascended Snowdon by this path. When Bwichysaethan was reached, Mrs. Gladstone declined to attempt the enormously steep climb to the top by way of the zig-zag path so auda- ciously cut in the face of Snowdon's supreme crag by Sir Edward Watkin' s engineers. A heavy cloud of mist just at the time swept over the top, and enshrouded it fora considerable time. Mr. Gladstone did not fear the steepness of the path, but when he saw the mist he yielded to the entreaties of Mrs. Gladstone and Mrs. Drew, and consented, not without regret, to proceed no further. Mrs. Drew and Mrs. Edgar Watkin, accom- panied by the guide, continued the upward journey The rest of the party, escorted by the sergeant and con- stable, returned to the house known as The Lodge. The evening was quietly spent indoors. To callers Mrs. Gladstone has expressed the utmost delight with the visit, both herself and Mr. Gladstone having enjoyed it thoroughly and been greatly invigorated by it.

The Liberal party in Liverpool are taking steps to- wards conferring the freedom of the city upon the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone, M.P. Mr. R. D. Holt, who is working energetically to carry out the proposal, has at last succeeded in receiving the support of many Tories, among others Alderman A. B. For wood, who opposed the proposition when it was brought forward in the City Council in December, 1891. It is not intended to bring the matter forward until the menthly meeting of the Council in October. ARRIVAL AT BARMOUTFI : MAGNIFICENT RECEPTION.

Mr. Gladstone, Mrs. Gladstone, the Rev. Stephen Gladstone, and Mrs. S. Gladstone arrived at Barmouth at twelve o'clock noon on Thursday, per special train from Portinadoc, under the charge of Mr. Alfred Aslett, general manager of the Cambrian Railway. The town was gaily decorated on the occasion, awl the shops and all places of business were closed in order to enable the inhabitants to accord the distinguished statesman an enthusiastic reception. On his arrival Mr. Gladstone and party were met at the railway station by the members of the local Committee and other gentlemen. On alighting, Mr. Gladstone was conducted to a carriage in waiting, and a procession was formed, headed by the above gentlemen, followed by the carriage ; then the school children, and after them the general public. On arrival at the Marine Hotel, where the distinguished , visitors will stay for the next six days, Mr. Gladstone was presented with an address of welcome and an album with photographs of local scenery. From a commodious platform in front of the hotel, the Premier delivered a speech, in which he referred to the facilities for the working classes to enjoy holidays in the present day to what existed some years ago. After touching upon various interesting topics, lie concluded by referring to the present Administration, and expressed a hope that the Government would be able to perform much beneficial work. MR. GLADSTONE AT BARMOITTR.

Mr. Gladstone's second day's visit to Barmouth has opened glorious as regards the weather. Early yester- day afternoon Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone took a long drive along the banks of the estuary of the Mawddach. As far as the 13armouth people are concerned, the expressed wish of the Premier as regards quietness, &c., will be strictly carried out.
