div.head: BUILDING SOCIETY FAILURE.
div.p: A BUILDING SOCIETY FAILURE.
The Sunderland Mutual Permanent Building Society, whose secretary, Alderman Lawson is alleged to have absconded, is being wound up. The liabilities are between £B,OOO and £9,000 and the assets £2,000

div.head: WRIT FOR LEEDS.
div.p: A WRIT FOR LEEDS.

The writ for South Leeds election was received yester- day, but the date for the nominations is not fixed. Mr. Mahon, Leeds, secretary to the General Labourers' Union, announces that he will contest the seat as a labour candidate.
DEATH OF A NOTED CO-OPERATOR.
Edward Vansittart Neale, of Marlow, the pioneer of the co-operative movement and formerly president of the Co-operative Association, died in London yesterday, aged 82.
"TOMMY" BURNS IN SCOTLAND.

Thomas Burns, aged twenty-five, the champion diver from Liverpool, was taken into custody by the Ayr police for diving into the tidal water from the New and Old Bridges. He was liberated on 40s hail, stating that he intended to dive from the Forth Bridge.

div.head: GAINSBOROUGH POISONING CASE.
div.p: GAINSBOROUGH POISONING CASE.

At the Gainsborouf.Th Police Court, yesterday, Alexan- der Morgan, fish dealer, was charged with the murder of Tom Morley, a Hull grocer, who died on the 16th ult. in a Gainsborough tavern from strychnine poisoning while in the accused's company. The analysis discloses that two grains of strychnine were found in deceased's stomach. The prisoner was finally committed for trial.

THE CHOLERA-LATEST DETAILS. Telegrams from Hamburg on Thursday were couched in a more hopeful tone. The last official return reports the occurrence of 282 fresh cases and 108 deaths, but of this number 79 cases and 27 deaths should properly. have been included in the previous day's return. At Altona five fresh cases have been declared, and one death is' announced. The House of Burgesses has voted the suns of £50,000 asked for by the Senate, and a eommittea has been appointed to investigate the sanitary clndition of the city, A Berlin correspondent states that no fresh case of cholera has occurred in the capital. There is at the same time considerable decrease in the number of patients being treated for choleraic dis?ases of a less serious character. From Antwerp the report is that three fresh cases and two deaths occurred on TOursia9. The victims were lightermen who were attacked on board their craft, and succumbed before reaching the. hospital.

CASE IN ENGLAND. On Thursday night the steamer Helene arrived at Grangemouth from Hamburg, and after being, examined by the sanitary authorities, was allowed to enter the dock. Yesterday, however, the second officer was re- moved to the hospital sufferirp, from illness, symptOra., of which point to cholera. The French railway companies have been notiliod that all luggage entering *Switzerland from France must be fumigated at the expense of the sender. Three deaths from cholera are reported to have occurred at Veules, watering place in Normandy. At Paris, Havre, and Rouen, the improvement continues. "I could never have loved any one else but Arthur. If we had never met, I ehould have gone unwedded to the grebe. I really believe, uncle, that a special Provi- dence brings abatt the meeting of the two who are destined to love each other. Do you remember the words of an old verse, which says: " ' Two shall meet the whole wide world apart, And speakAn different tongues, and have no'need Each of the other's being, and no thought; And these to unknown lands, o'er unknown seas, shall cross, Escaping wreck, defying death, and all unconsciously,. - Shape every act to this one end': That one day out of darkness they shall meet, . And read life's meaning in each other's eyes. And this is fate, or destiny.'" , CHAPTER XIV. "I LOVE HIM WITH ALL 'MY HEART," THE GIRL FILID, SRYLY, BOWING RER DARK CURLY HEAD CONFUSEDLY. "You need not be afraid that I shall ever rue it, uncle," she went on, eagerly, " for I never shall. With me, to love once, is to love for ever. I shall love Arthur faithfully all my life, and when I come to die his mune shall be the last on my lips. "Why, how you are trembling, uncle 1 Are you Ill?" Colonel Whitney forced a smile to his lips, but his mental agony was so intense it died away in a groan of despair. He pushed -the soft, white, clinging arms and the beautiful face from him, striding desperately tip and down the room. . "Oh, uncle, are you ill ?" sokbed lonie, standing before him with terror-blanched face and clasped hands. , "No—yes 1 For, the love of Heaven, leave me alone, lonic 1" he cried out. "My torture is great —great!" "If you are ill—in pain—my place is by your side, uncle," she declared. "Do let me stay! Do let me help you 1 You know I love you 60 *CH I would give my very life for you, my dearest uncle," Ile stopped short and looked at her, his eyes burn- ing fitfully. She "would give her very life for him, she loved him so!" How strangely these wads fell, upon his startled ear. "In Heaven's name, leave me to myself I " he cried. "I cannot bear it. Go, my dear; if I want you I will call you." Wondering, and just a little grieved, lonie turned and quitted the room very slowly. In the corridor she met Miss Carriscourt, and to her she related what had transpired. "The colonel seems very 'ill," she remarl:ed, thoeightfully ; "I have noticed it for a week past,". 1 n thsve you ?" asked lonie, quickly, and her hran , smote her i.O think that she had been so completely l engrossed in ter own happiness that she had not noticed it. I , " lie seems like a person labouring under great mental excitement," pursued the lady. "I noticed to-day at luncheon that his hands trembled so vio- lently he could not raise his tea-cup to his lips. a fli,n;el in a very, short time, is apt to bring on Waits 4ver-r. . Greatly frightened, lonic went back at puce to the library and noiselessly Opel:Lea !Ito do= .( I Was it only fancy, or did she hear the colonel moan out sharply: - "I cannot! I will not wreck her happiness, though the cost be death to me! She loves him. Let them be happy. The horrible -temptation is over. lonic shall not be sacrificed ! She shall marry Arthur Rochester I" . 1 She crossed the room quickly, her footfalls making I no sound on the thick velvet carpet. , Reaching his side, she knelt on the hassock ab his feet and laid a little hand on his arm. " Uncle," she said, gently, " something is the matter. There is something terribly wrong. You. are ill, or in great trouble. Won't you confide in me?" Colonel Whitney raised his grey, haggard face, and looked into the beautiful, pleading, girlish one. 'Oh, if I dared tell you, 'lonic!" he moaned, huskily. "But no, it must not be; your verdict might be against rue; you might hate me, and that would kill me." "Hate you, uncle l" lonic repeated, in amaze- ment. " Ah, you know that that could never be. What de I not owe to your kindness, your generosity? But for you, I should now be earning my own bread in some workshop or factory, from the rising of the sun till the setting of it. You have taken me from a tenement house and placed me in a mansion. Believe me, uncle, my gratitude shall end only with my life. You grieve me by even imagining that my love could ever be shaken." Strong man though he was, he bowed his head and wept like a child. "Oh, lonie, if I dared confide in you, child?" he repeated. A sudden thought came to Joule. She leaned over him, impulsively kissing him. "Have ydu had any great loss in business, uncle r she whispered. "The loss of money which will make you bankrupt? lam only a young girl, but I have heard of such things. It that is it, do not grieve, uncle. Money will not buy everything. It cannot purchase happiness." "It is not the loss of money, lonic," he groaned. "I am a rich man; but in this case money will not help me. It is like so much dross—it is powerless." He rose abruptly from his chair and paced hurriedly up and down the length of the room, with hands clenched, and great drops of moisture gather- ing on his brow, then as abruptly sank down in his chair again, covering his face with his trembling hands. "Though the whole world should turn against me, would you be true—steadfast and true 2' he asked hoarsely. Those words amazed her. " How strange to hear such words as those from his lips," she thought. "Just as if the world, as you phrase it, could ever turn against you, uncle," she declared, warmly. "Why, there never was a man more universally respected, honoured, and beloved. Your life has been a remarkably noble one, an example for good and true men to follow. There is not a little news- boy or bootblack on the street but what cries as you pass: ' There goes Colonel Whitney, the friend of the poor!' And the working men respond, 'Yes, he's our friend! God bless him I— " Why will you remind me of this, Ionic?" cried. the colonel, in agony. "You torture me inexpres- sibly." "I simply want to remind you how dearly you are beloved by your fellow-men," answered lonie. "Then you can see for yourself that the idea of people turning against you is simply preposterous. Why should they ?" "That is the terrible secret that is eating my life out, child," fie responded, bitterly. "lonic," he added, "you are too young to know all that a vow imports; but you understand its solemnity." With beautiful, wondering eyes, she answered: "Yes." "if you will register a vow to me that you will never divulge one word of what I may say to you here and now, I will tell you my story," said Colonel Whitney. "But you must swear that you will never repeat one word of it to any human being, never one word to your lover." Pale and trembling, lonic Lawrence looked at him. "I am afraid," she said, "I have never sworn in all my life. Let me promise that I will do as you wish, uncle. That will meet the case as well. I. shall keep my word." "No, you must swear it, lonic. For the rest of my life I shall trust no one—neither man, woman, nor child. Every promise made me shall be bound by an oath. You need not tremble, child; many people take oaths." "But if I break it 2 " the girl asked, piteously. "That is the very thing," he said. "How could I be sure of your eternal silence, when you are not even sure of yourself? You must swear not to reveal one word of my story, under any cause or circumstance; then I shall rest content, for you will always bear in mind the punishment that will follow if you do not keep your oath." The lovely young face grew as pale as a white lily. "If you desire me to do it, uncle, I will, for it must be right," she answered, slowly. And he was satisfied. "You are sure the door is closed, lonie," he asked, anxiously, "and that no one is listening outside?" And she saw him tremble at the very thought. "Your servants are too honest for that, uncle," she said, gently. "A chance word overheard might ruin me, child," he gasped. "Sit down on this hassock at my feet; let me look into your beautiful eyes, and it will give me strepgtb to proceed." gi rllotnhieens. at When nn she dariroescet efdr 0. mSthhea twhaasssao ck Happythe 1 bitterness of death was at her heart, for her young life would be wrecked against the sharp rock of 1 fate, and her future would be a dreary blank, with but one hope in it—and that was that Heaven, in its infinite mercy would send her—death. For one moment Colonel Whitney held the little white hand tremblingly in his.
